tom_tat: In this age of decline, the moral standard of humanity sinks lower with each passing day, while wrongdoing grows ever greater. Drawn forth by the collective karma of the majority, calamities arise all over the world: earthquakes, storms, floods, volcanoes, and more.
noi_dung:
Foreword

We live in an age of decline: the moral standard of humanity sinks lower each day, while wrongdoing grows ever greater. Moved by the collective karma of the majority, the whole world is shaken by earthquakes, storms, floods, volcanoes, droughts, and unseasonable weather. Compared with only a few decades ago, the killing, robbery, lust, and fraud rampant today fill all who care about the moral life of the world with dread! The sutras say: "All suffering and joy are made by the mind." To improve people and create better conditions, we must begin by reforming the very source. That is to say, everyone must cut off evil thoughts — just as one who wants clear water must not let the spring run muddy.

While reading the Si Gui Ji (Reflections on Returning Home), I found it beneficial for turning people's hearts toward goodness and toward the path of liberation, so outside my hours of Buddha-recitation I translated it, one passage at a time, into this volume, Fragrance of the Homeland of Ultimate Bliss. Though its exhortations go no further than doing good and reciting the Buddha's name, these are precisely the skillful means that lead people deep into genuine practice, silently and wondrously transforming both people and their circumstances. For those who deeply understand the Dharma, every phenomenon is principle, and practice in the midst of phenomena is itself practice of the principle. Conversely, to prize theory alone without caring for genuine practice is mere empty theory that yields no fruit.

Long ago, there was a monk who, wherever he went to teach the Dharma, spoke only of taking refuge in the Three Jewels. Someone asked why he never taught anything else. He replied: "Consider — is there any Dharma outside the scope of the Three Jewels?" In our country, the common cultivation of monastic and lay Buddhists likewise comes down to this: keeping the precepts, understanding cause and effect, doing good, and reciting the Buddha's name. Even many deeply learned Buddhists arrive at this same point in the end. So a single sentence of Buddha-recitation, if practiced with singleness of mind, can hardly be called insufficient. Reading this volume, you will receive the golden words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and the firsthand cultivation experience of wise teachers of goodness — no different from having good teachers and good friends beside you. If you truly practice according to the teachings found here, you will gain three great benefits:

1. Through the protection of the Buddhas, the power of the merit of Buddha-recitation, and the power of your own wholesome thoughts, you yourself will dissolve karmic obstacles, increase blessings and wisdom, and be spared many of the perils and disasters of this Dharma-ending age.

2. Through these same three powers, the shared suffering of humanity can be lessened, if many people keep a vegetarian diet and recite the Buddha's name. Thus, though cultivating the Western Pure Land, one is at the same time cultivating a human Pure Land right here in this world.

3. By single-mindedly reciting the Buddha's name, you will be reborn in Ultimate Bliss, escaping entirely the suffering of samsara, enjoying boundless and endless bliss, and in time realizing the fruit of the Path and liberating sentient beings. This is a way to benefit both self and others, complete and certain.

Following the Chinese original, this volume has been supplemented and reprinted many times. Thus, although its preface was written by Master Yinguang in the 28th year of the Republic (1938), a later section adds his teachings, his biography (he passed away in 1940), and that of Great Master Hongyi (who passed away in 1942). Readers are asked to understand this and not take it as grounds for doubt.

In translating this volume, I have been moved by the heaviness of the world's suffering and the decline of the true teaching. Reflecting on what heavy karmic obstacles of mine caused me to be born in this degenerate age, and by what blessings I came to hear the sound of the Dharma, I could not bear to keep its benefit for myself alone. According to my strength and my share, I proclaim the path of liberation to repay the four kindnesses and to bring joy and benefit to all beings, however little that may be.

"Long adrift, I pity the lonely traveler;

I would urge my fellow beings to return to our homeland!"

I borrow these two lines of verse to express my own feelings.

Retreat season, year of Canh Ty (1960)

Translator: Lien Du, respectfully recorded

Preface

The Pure Land Dharma-door is lofty beyond measure, vast as heaven sheltering and earth bearing all. It is the all-embracing Dharma-door of the Buddhas of the three times, the special wondrous path within Shakyamuni Buddha's entire lifetime of teaching. Above, even Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment cannot go beyond its scope; below, even those who have committed the gravest rebellious evils may share in its deliverance.

Yet precisely because this Dharma-door is so lofty while its embrace is so universal — using little effort yet reaping swift and immense results — those with a smattering of learning in the Chan and doctrinal schools look down on it as a practice for ignorant men and women. At bottom, this is because they do not yet understand the great and small, the difficult and easy, of self-power versus the Buddha's power. The superiority of one over the other truly cannot be fully depicted in words. Why?

Because every other Dharma-door relies on the power of precepts, meditation, and wisdom, cultivating until karma is cleansed and afflictions are emptied before one can escape the birth and death of samsara. But how easy is that state of cleansed karma and emptied afflictions to attain? Among the two kinds of delusion, cutting off delusions of view is as hard as holding back a flood racing forty miles — let alone delusions of thought! Even a highly awakened person of superior understanding, if afflictions are not fully severed, still falls back into samsara. And once reborn, among ten thousand backsliders there may be scarcely one advancer in a hundred million — three or four at most. Self-power is thus not enough to rely on; it offers nothing firm. Should those who boast of their wisdom and refuse to follow the Tathagata's compassionate vow to gather in all beings feel proud of themselves?

As for the Pure Land door alone: if one has complete and genuine faith and vows, and with utter sincerity recites the Buddha's name as a child remembers its mother, while daily conduct never strays from the moral path, then at life's end one will be received by the Buddha and reborn in the West. Even though such a person's delusions of karma may remain, once reborn there what is attained surpasses even an Arhat whose afflictions are emptied and karma cleansed — for their seed-natures differ. If this is true of one whose delusions are not yet severed, no more need be said of one whose karma is already exhausted! This is due to the Buddha's power, the Dharma's power, and the power of sentient beings' own minds — all inconceivable; and the mind's power, supported by the power of the Buddha and the Dharma, is revealed in utter completeness. To rely only on self-power, compared with relying on the Buddha's power, falls as far short as heaven is from earth, by countless Ganges-sands of difference! Know too that the principle of this Pure Land door cannot be judged together with ordinary Dharma-doors, for it is a special Dharma-door! I often offer this couplet:

A lofty Dharma-door, benefiting all three capacities — whereby the nine realms return together, praised by the ten directions.

A vast and deep Buddha-vow, refusing no being — hence a thousand sutras point to it, ten thousand treatises proclaim it.

In the Avatamsaka Sutra's chapter on Samantabhadra's Practices and Vows, all the Dharma-body Great Beings of the forty-one stages (the Ten Abodes, Ten Practices, Ten Dedications, Ten Grounds, and Equal Enlightenment) in the ocean of worlds of the Flower Treasury, following Samantabhadra Bodhisattva's encouragement, dedicate the merit of the ten great kings of vows to seek rebirth in the West, so as to perfectly realize Buddhahood. If such great beings act so, then we ordinary beings laden with karma — relying on a scrap of talent and resolve, despising the Pure Land door — should ask ourselves: are we superior to those Bodhisattvas? Or, bewildered and grasping at heights, do we seek transcendence only to fall, seek cleverness only to prove clumsy?

The books proclaiming the Pure Land, past and present, are very many. Among them, Great Master Ru Cen selected the finest words and noble ideas of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Patriarchs, and the discourses of wise teachers of recent times, and compiled them into this Fragrance of the Homeland of Ultimate Bliss (a free rendering of the two words Si Gui, "longing for home"). The Great Master asked me to write a preface. Reflecting that in youth I did not strive, and now in old age and failing powers I can only set down, to discharge my duty, the meaning I have believed and understood over fifty-nine years, I take the occasion to offer this small token of sincerity, vowing that all fellow beings may alike be reborn in Ultimate Bliss. That is my true heart; as for talented critics who may mock it, I have never given them a thought. With this, I offer a few lines of song:

"I urge all to give rise together to wholesome vows, vowing rebirth in the Pure Land. In a foreign land, streams and mountains are full of peril — let who will cling to them in affection! If you yourself do not wish to return, so be it; but be resolved, and you will surely arrive. On the homeward road, who contends with you — cool breeze and bright moon!"

Travelers longing for home, take heed!

28th year of the Republic, year of Ky Mao, Winter Solstice season.

Shakyamuni Yinguang, respectfully composed

tom_tat: (Shakyamuni Muni is Sanskrit, rendered as the Able, the Benign, and the Silent One: Shakya is the clan name, Muni the given name; Buddha means the Awakened One. Our Fundamental Teacher was once Prince Siddhartha of Central India, in the kingdom of Kapilavastu — his father King Shuddhodana, his mother Queen Maya. The Prince left home at nineteen, attained enlightenment at thirty, taught for fifty years, and lived to eighty. The Buddha appeared in the world to liberate countless beings, and today his teaching is honored across Asia and Europe.)
noi_dung:
Shakyamuni Buddha

(Shakyamuni Muni is Sanskrit, rendered as the Able, the Benign, and the Silent One: Shakya is the clan name, Muni the given name; Buddha means the Awakened One. Our Fundamental Teacher was once Prince Siddhartha of Central India, in the kingdom of Kapilavastu — his father King Shuddhodana, his mother Queen Maya. The Prince left home at nineteen, attained enlightenment at thirty, taught for fifty years, and lived to eighty. The Buddha appeared in the world to liberate countless beings, and today his teaching is honored across Asia and Europe.)

The Buddha Speaks of Amitabha Sutra says: "From here, going straight west, past a hundred thousand million Buddha-lands, there is a world called Ultimate Bliss. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitabha, who is even now teaching the Dharma. — Why is that land called Ultimate Bliss? Because the beings there suffer no pain but enjoy every bliss; hence it is called Ultimate Bliss. — And why is that Buddha named Amitabha? Because this Buddha's light is immeasurable, shining throughout the lands of the ten directions without obstruction anywhere; hence the name Amitabha. Moreover, that Buddha and his people live for immeasurable, boundless asamkhya kalpas; hence the name Amitabha. — Beings reborn in Ultimate Bliss are all of the stage of non-retrogression; among them are a great many in the stage of One Birth More, beyond all reckoning by number — describable only as immeasurable, boundless asamkhyas. — Beings who hear this sutra should vow to be reborn in that land. — Why? Because there they will dwell together with such superior good people. — If good men or good women hear of Amitabha Buddha and hold his name in mindfulness, for one day, two days, three days, up to seven days, with mind unconfused, then when their lives end, Amitabha Buddha with his host of sages will appear before them. Their minds then free from delusion, they will at once be reborn in Ultimate Bliss. — All you beings! You should believe this sutra, praised as 'of inconceivable merit, protected and kept in mind by all Buddhas.'

• The Great Assembly Sutra says: "The practitioner sits upright and single-mindedly contemplates Amitabha Buddha — such his beauty, such his bearing, such his assembly, such his teaching. Contemplating thus, thought following upon thought in unbroken succession without confusion, one will see that Buddha. It is like a man or woman of this world, far away in a distant land, dreaming of their own home. At that moment, they truly know not night from day, inside from outside; walls, cliffs, and mountains cannot block them, and even pitch darkness cannot hinder them. If the practitioner trains in recollection thought after thought in this way, in time contemplation will grow lucid and keen, and as a result one will behold Amitabha Buddha."

• The Sutra of Sixteen Contemplations says: —To be reborn in Ultimate Bliss, one must cultivate three kinds of blessings: 1) serve one's parents with filial care, attend one's teachers, keep a compassionate mind that harms no life, and cultivate the ten wholesome deeds; 2) take the Three Refuges, keep all the precepts in full, and never violate the codes of deportment; 3) give rise to the mind of enlightenment, believe deeply in the principle of cause and effect, recite the Mahayana sutras, and encourage others in cultivation. These three are called pure karma.

• The Ratnakuta Sutra says: —At that time Maitreya Bodhisattva said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One! As you have spoken of the meritorious benefits of Amitabha Buddha and the land of Ultimate Bliss, and have said: if any being gives rise to the ten kinds of resolve and single-mindedly recites with whole heart directed toward Amitabha Buddha, then at life's end that person will be reborn in that Buddha's world. World-Honored One! What are these ten kinds of resolve, by which resolve one is reborn in Ultimate Bliss?" —The Buddha said: "Maitreya! These ten resolves cannot be made by ordinary, unwholesome people. What are the ten:

Toward beings, give rise to great kindness that inflicts no harm.

Toward beings, give rise to great compassion that causes no distress.

Toward the Buddha's true Dharma, give rise to a guarding heart that would not spare even life itself.

Toward all wholesome dharmas, give rise to superior forbearance, free from attachment.

A mind joyful, pure, and reverent, free from greed for gain and homage.

A mind seeking the Buddha's wisdom, never distracted at any time.

Toward all beings, constant reverence and respect, never despising any as lowly.

Not indulging in worldly discourse; toward the enlightenment portion, a resolute mind.

A pure mind cultivating all roots of goodness, never defiled.

Toward all Tathagatas, casting off all marks, a mind of constant recollection.

Maitreya! These are the ten resolves of a Bodhisattva; by such resolve one is reborn in Amitabha Buddha's land of Ultimate Bliss. Maitreya! If among these ten resolves one accomplishes even a single one as one wishes, delighting in rebirth in Ultimate Bliss, it cannot be that rebirth there is not attained.

Our Teacher Amitabha Buddha

(Amitabha is Sanskrit, rendered as Immeasurable Life or Immeasurable Light. He is the teaching lord of the land of Ultimate Bliss in the West. According to the Sutra of the King of Ancient Voices, in a past age there was a kingdom of Wonderful Joy whose king was named Kusika. At that time a Buddha called Free King appeared in the world. Kusika left home under that Buddha with the name Dharmakara. And the Sutra of Immeasurable Life says: "The monk Dharmakara, before the Buddha Lokesvararaja, gave rise to the mind of enlightenment and made forty-eight vows, each vow declaring: 'If it is not so, I vow not to become a Buddha.'

Those great vows have been fulfilled, and Dharmakara has become a Buddha — Amitabha of the present land of Ultimate Bliss.)

*According to the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, among Amitabha Buddha's forty-eight great vows, several are especially essential:

Vow 18 — When I become a Buddha, if beings of the ten directions, with wholehearted joyful faith, wish to be reborn in my land and call my name even ten times, and yet are not reborn there, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.

Vow 19 — When I become a Buddha, if beings of the ten directions give rise to the mind of enlightenment, cultivate merit, and wholeheartedly vow to be reborn in my land, then at life's end, if I do not appear before them with my host of sages to receive them, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.

Vow 21 — When I become a Buddha, if the humans and gods of my land are not all endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great being, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.

Vow 27 — When I become a Buddha, from humans and gods down to every thing in my land, all forms shall be beautiful, solemn, pure, radiant, and wondrous to the utmost, beyond reckoning. If beings who have attained the divine eye could clearly reckon their number, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.

Vow 32 — When I become a Buddha, from the ground up to the sky, the palaces, towers, ponds, trees, and flowers — all myriad things — shall be made of immeasurable jewels and hundreds of thousands of fragrant blossoms joined together, solemnly beautiful and marvelous beyond all heavenly palaces. The fragrance of my land shall spread through the worlds of the ten directions, and Bodhisattvas who encounter it shall all cultivate the Buddha's practices. If it is not so, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.

Vow 39 — When I become a Buddha, the humans and gods of my land shall all enjoy bliss like monks rid of all outflows. If it is not so, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.

noi_dung:
Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva

In the Sutra of the Compassionate Lotus, in a past kalpa during the age of Buddha Ratnagarbha, when Amitabha was still a wheel-turning king, the Bodhisattva was his eldest crown prince, named Bat Thuan. When the Prince had made his great vow before Buddha Ratnagarbha, the Buddha bestowed on him the name Avalokiteshvara. At present, the Bodhisattva dwells in Ultimate Bliss, assisting Amitabha Buddha in teaching and in receiving beings. In the future, the Bodhisattva will succeed Amitabha as a Buddha, named King of the Mountain of All Merits Manifesting Everywhere; the land of Ultimate Bliss will be renamed Accomplished of All Precious Jewels.

As for the Bodhisattva's causal practices, resultant virtues, and responsive manifestations, the Lotus Sutra, the Shurangama Sutra, and the Great Compassion Sutra all speak of them.)

• The Great Compassion Dharani Sutra says: "If one single-mindedly invokes the name of and makes offerings to our Fundamental Teacher Amitabha Buddha, one will gain immeasurable blessings, erase immeasurable offenses, and at life's end be reborn in Ultimate Bliss. At that moment the Tathagata will extend his hand to receive that person and stroke his crown, saying: 'Do not be afraid, for you have been reborn in my land.'

• The Sutra of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's Prediction says: "Whoever gives rise to the supreme mind of enlightenment and vows rebirth in Ultimate Bliss will behold that land, and behold Amitabha Buddha together with the ranks of Bodhisattvas and Hearers. Seeing this, that person will rejoice with leaping joy and proclaim: 'Nam Mô A Di Đà Như Lai, Ứng Cúng, Chánh Biến Tri!' At that time, in the Dharma assembly, 84,000 beings will all give rise to the mind of enlightenment, vowing to plant roots of goodness so as to be reborn in Ultimate Bliss.

---o0o---

noi_dung:
Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva

In the Sutra of the Compassionate Lotus, in a past kalpa during the age of Buddha Ratnagarbha, when Amitabha was still a wheel-turning king, the Bodhisattva was his second crown prince, named Mani. When Prince Mani had made his vow of oath before Buddha Ratnagarbha, the Buddha bestowed on him the name Attainer of Great Power, and predicted that he would later become a Buddha named Well-Abiding King of the Mountain of Precious Jewels. At present, the Bodhisattva dwells in Ultimate Bliss, assisting Amitabha Buddha in teaching and in receiving beings. In the future the Bodhisattva will become a Buddha succeeding Avalokiteshvara, with a world, kalpas, and Buddha-works the same as those of Buddha King of the Mountain of Merits. In the Shurangama Sutra, the Bodhisattva teaches a Buddha-recitation Dharma-door that is truly most pure; cultivators of pure karma should follow it.)

• The Shurangama Sutra says: "I remember, countless Ganges-sands of kalpas ago, twelve Tathagatas appeared in succession within one kalpa, the first named Immeasurable Light and the last named Surpassing Sun-and-Moon Light. That last Buddha taught me the Buddha-recitation samadhi. It is like two people: one always remembers, the other always forgets — though the two meet, it is as if they never meet, though they see, as if they never see. If both remember each other, the power of memory growing ever deeper, then from this life to the next the two are as form and shadow, never parting. The Tathagatas of the ten directions are mindful of beings as a mother remembers her child — yet if the child keeps running away, what can the mother do, for all her remembering! Conversely, if the child remembers its mother as the mother remembers the child, then mother and child will never be parted, life after life. If the minds of beings constantly remember and recite the Buddha, then in this life and the next they will surely behold the Buddha, never far from the Buddha, with no need of any other expedient — their own minds will be opened to enlightenment. As one who dyes cloth in fragrance will carry that scent upon the body, so this is adornment with fragrant light. My own root cause was to attain the Forbearance of the Unborn through a mind that recites the Buddha; now in this land I gather in those who recite the Buddha and bring them to the Pure Land. Now that the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, I make no selection: gathering in the six senses, with pure recitation in unbroken succession, I attain samadhi — this is foremost."

---o0o---

noi_dung:
Manjushri Bodhisattva

(Manjushri is also rendered Manjughosha, translated as Wondrous Virtue or Wondrous Auspiciousness. According to the Sutra of the Compassionate Lotus, the Bodhisattva was once Prince Vuong Chung, the third son of the wheel-turning king during the age of Buddha Ratnagarbha. When the Prince had made his vast vow before the Buddha, his name was changed to Manjushri, and he received the prediction that he would later become a Buddha named Universal Manifestation, in the world Pure and Stainless of Precious Branches in the south. And the Sutra of Manjushri's Parinirvana says: "Manjushri Bodhisattva manifested birth in the country of Shravasti, in the village of Da La, as the son of the brahmin Pham Duc, emerging from his mother's right side, his body the color of purple gold, able to speak at that very moment. Grown, he left home under the Buddha.")

• The Avatamsaka Sutra says: "At that time, light shone through a thousand worlds, and all the Manjushris of those lands simultaneously spoke this verse before the Buddha: 'In every dignified bearing, ever mindful of the Buddha's merits, day and night unceasing — such karma should be cultivated.'

• The Sutra of the Ocean of Contemplating the Buddha Samadhi says: "After abandoning his former causes, this Manjushri Bodhisattva declared himself to have attained Buddha-recitation samadhi and to be certain of rebirth in the Pure Land; the World-Honored One predicted: 'You shall be reborn in Ultimate Bliss.' The Bodhisattva then spoke this vow in verse:

"I vow that at life's end, removing every obstacle, I shall behold Amitabha Buddha and be reborn in Ultimate Bliss. Once arrived there, I shall fulfill all my great vows, and Amitabha, the World-Honored One, shall predict my Buddhahood."

• The Records of Pure Land Sages and Worthies says: "In the Tang dynasty, Great Master Fazhao was gathered by Manjushri's spiritual power into the sacred realm on Mount Wutai. The Great Master bowed to the Bodhisattva and asked for the essential door of cultivation. Manjushri said: 'You should now recite the Buddha's name — it is exactly the timely practice, for among all doors of cultivation none surpasses Buddha-recitation. Diligently make offerings to the Three Jewels and cultivate both blessings and wisdom together; these two are most essential. In past lives I attained Omniscience through making offerings, contemplation, and Buddha-recitation. Thus all dharmas — the perfection of wisdom, the deepest meditation doors, even the Buddhas themselves — are all born from Buddha-recitation. Know then that Buddha-recitation is the king of all dharmas.' Fazhao asked: 'How should your disciple recite?' The Bodhisattva said: 'In the western world there is Amitabha Buddha. That Buddha's vow-power is inconceivable; you should be mindful of him without interruption, and at life's end you will surely be reborn there, never to retrogress.' Speaking thus, the Bodhisattva stroked Fazhao's crown with his golden arm and said: 'Through your Buddha-recitation, before long you shall realize supreme enlightenment.' The Great Master, having received the prediction, joyfully bowed and withdrew.

---o0o---

noi_dung:
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva

(According to the Sutra of the Compassionate Lotus, the Bodhisattva was once Prince Van Do, the eighth son of the wheel-turning king during the age of Buddha Ratnagarbha. After the Prince had made his great vow before the Buddha, his name was changed to Samantabhadra, and he received the prediction that he would later become a Buddha named King of the Diamond-Willed Banner of Sovereign Marks, in the world Pure Merit Abiding in Wisdom-Water in the north. And according to the Avatamsaka Sutra, the Bodhisattva, already the left-hand assistant of Buddha Vairocana, still used the ten great kings of vows to guide the ocean-wide assembly of Bodhisattvas in the Flower Treasury to rebirth together in Ultimate Bliss. Shall we, who are lowly mortals, not vow to follow suit?)

• The Avatamsaka Sutra says: "When Samantabhadra Bodhisattva had praised the Tathagata's supreme merits, he addressed the Bodhisattvas and Sudhana: 'To accomplish such merit, one must cultivate ten vast practices and vows.

Worship the Buddhas

Praise the Tathagatas

Cultivate offerings abundantly

Repent karmic obstacles

Rejoice in all merits

Request the Buddhas to turn the Dharma-wheel

Request the Buddhas to remain in the world

Ever follow the Buddhas in training

Constantly accord with beings

Dedicate all merit universally.

If anyone with deep faith upholds, recites, and copies even four lines of this great vow, the offenses of the five uninterrupted sins will swiftly be erased. When that person reaches life's end, in the final instant, though all the senses disintegrate, this great vow alone will never part from them, and they will at once be reborn in Ultimate Bliss."

• The Sutra of the Tathagata's Inconceivable State says: "If one seeks supreme enlightenment and single-mindedly cultivates one practice to completion, one will surely succeed. It is like drinking a handful of water from the great sea — one has thereby drunk all the river waters of Jambudvipa. If a Bodhisattva can cultivate this door of mindfulness of the Buddha, the sea of enlightenment, then one has cultivated all samadhis, all forbearances, all grounds, all dharanis."

---o0o---

noi_dung:
Ashvaghosha Bodhisattva

(According to the Transmission of the Lamp, when the Bodhisattva was born, even herds of horses were moved to wail in grief. The Bodhisattva was so skilled at teaching that horses hearing him would shed tears and cry out. Six hundred years after Shakyamuni's passing, the ninety-six non-Buddhist schools of the Western Regions all revived and attacked the Dharma; the Bodhisattva then manifested birth in Eastern India, in the country of Sangkida, composing many treatises to reveal the true and refute the false. In his Awakening of Faith, the Bodhisattva urges people to recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the West. At life's end, he entered the samadhi of the Dragon's Vigorous Advance, rose into the sky emitting radiance brilliant as the sun, then returned to his seat and entered nirvana.)

• The Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana says: "One should vigorously exert oneself: six times day and night, bow to the Buddhas; sincerely repent, invite, rejoice, and dedicate toward the fruit of enlightenment. Cultivating thus without rest, one will escape all obstacles and roots of goodness will grow." It also says: "The Tathagata has a direct expedient for embracing the faithful: through single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha, following one's vow to seek rebirth in another direction's Pure Land — for by constantly beholding the Buddha, one is forever parted from the evil paths. As a sutra says: 'If one single-mindedly recites Amitabha Buddha of the West and dedicates the roots of goodness one has cultivated toward that land, one will be reborn there. Through constantly beholding the Buddha, there is no more fear of retrogression.'

---o0o---

Nagarjuna Bodhisattva

(He is called Nagarjuna because he was born beneath a tree where nagas dwelt, and realized the Path in the Naga Palace. The Bodhisattva was of brahmin lineage, a native of Southern India, broadly learned in all worldly studies; within three months of leaving home he had mastered the Tripitaka. The Naga King then invited him down to the Naga Palace, where in nine weeks he read not even a ten-thousandth of the Naga Treasury, and awakened to the forbearance of the unborn. Returning to the human realm, the Bodhisattva spread the Buddha's teaching and composed the Dasabhumika-vibhasa, in which he urges people to recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the West. Later he entered the samadhi of the Vow Wheel and passed away. In the Lankavatara Sutra the Buddha prophetically declared: "South of India, a monk Nagarjuna shall appear, who will illuminate the meaning of the Middle Way, realize the First Joyful Ground, and be reborn in Ultimate Bliss.")

• The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says: "Buddha-recitation samadhi can dispel all afflictions and offenses of former lives. Moreover, Buddha-recitation samadhi carries great blessings that can liberate beings. Thus if Bodhisattvas wishing to liberate beings cultivate other samadhis, they cannot match the door of Buddha-recitation samadhi, for this door carries great blessings and swiftly extinguishes offenses. The Buddha is the Dharma-king, the Bodhisattva the Dharma-minister; what the Bodhisattva honors is the Buddha alone, the World-Honored One. The Bodhisattva ever skillfully cultivates the causes of Buddha-mindfulness, and thus ever meets the Buddhas — as the Pratyutpanna Sutra says: 'A Bodhisattva entering this samadhi is at once born manifest in Amitabha Buddha's land.'

• The Dasabhumika-vibhasa says: "Amitabha has this primal vow: 'If one calls my name and takes refuge in me, that person shall surely attain supreme enlightenment.' Therefore one must cherish and recite the Buddha." And he praised the Buddha in verse:

Wisdom bright, immeasurable.

Body like a throne of golden mountains.

With body, mouth, and mind,

Palms joined, I bow my head.

The Buddha's feet with thousand-spoked wheels,

Soft and gentle as lotus petals —

All who see them rejoice;

I bow my head at the Buddha's feet.

The white curl's mark, radiant and fair,

Pure as the autumn moon,

Its light glowing on his golden face —

Therefore I bow my head.

If one would become a Buddha,

With mind recite Amitabha;

In due time manifesting a body for them —

Therefore I take refuge.

One who calls upon the Buddha —

Merit's power immeasurable —

At once enters samadhi.

Therefore I ever recite.

If one plants roots of goodness,

With doubt, the flower will not open;

One whose faithful heart is pure —

The flower opens, at once beholding the Buddha.

Through this blessed cause,

One shall surely gain supreme excellence;

I vow all kinds of beings

Shall likewise all attain it.

---o0o---

tom_tat: (The Bodhisattva was a native of India. Newly ordained, he studied the Lesser Vehicle and slandered the Mahayana scriptures. Later, through his elder brother Asanga's repeated guidance, he repented his error and wished to cut out his own tongue. Asanga said: 'Long ago you used your tongue to slander the Mahayana; now you must use your tongue to praise it and redeem your offense...')
noi_dung:
Vasubandhu Bodhisattva

(The Bodhisattva was a native of India. Newly ordained, he studied the Lesser Vehicle and slandered the Mahayana scriptures. Later, through his elder brother Asanga's repeated guidance, he repented his error and wished to cut out his own tongue. Asanga said: "Long ago you used your tongue to slander the Mahayana; now you must use your tongue to praise that Dharma and redeem your offense. It is not yet too late to mend your fault — what good would cutting out your tongue do?" Obeying his brother, Vasubandhu devoted his whole heart to composing more than a hundred Mahayana treatises. Among them is the Treatise on Rebirth, which illuminates the adornments and benefits of the Pure Land. Those who recite the Buddha's name should pay heed to this treatise.)

• The Treatise on the Sutra of Immeasurable Life says: "If one cultivates the five gates of mindfulness to completion, the result will be rebirth in Ultimate Bliss, beholding Amitabha Buddha. What are the five gates of mindfulness?

The gate of worship

The gate of praise

The gate of vowing

The gate of contemplation

The gate of dedication.

What is worship? It is to bow with the body to Amitabha Buddha, expressing reverence and seeking the Buddha's embrace.

What is the gate of praise? It is to praise with the mouth the bodily marks, the name and meaning, the light and wisdom of that Tathagata, wishing to cultivate in truth so as to correspond with them.

What is the gate of vowing? It is to single-mindedly enter right concentration, vowing rebirth in Ultimate Bliss.

What is contemplation? It is to contemplate with right mindfulness the adorned merits of Ultimate Bliss, the adorned merits of Amitabha Buddha, and the adorned merits of the Bodhisattvas and the holy assembly.

What is dedication? It is, with a compassionate heart that abandons no suffering being, to dedicate one's own roots of goodness and merit, vowing that all sentient beings alike be reborn in Ultimate Bliss.

---o0o---

tom_tat: (According to the Precise Pointers to the West, the Bodhisattva describes his own past causes thus: 'Long ago, under King Ming of the Jin dynasty, I was a pauper. Pitying my own plight, I made a great vow: 'Due to past karma I suffer this retribution of poverty...')
noi_dung:
Bodhisattva Jiaoming Miaoxing

(According to the Precise Pointers to the West, the Bodhisattva describes his own past causes thus: "Long ago, under King Ming of the Jin dynasty, I was a pauper. Pitying my own plight, I made a great vow: 'Due to past karma I suffer this retribution of poverty. From now on I vow to recite the Buddha's name in cultivation; if I do not behold Amitabha Buddha and be reborn in Ultimate Bliss to accomplish all merits, then even if this body is shattered, I will not give up.' Having vowed, for seven days and nights I recollected with concentrated vigor, and my mind opened: I beheld Amitabha Buddha's bodily marks, beautiful and radiant, filling the worlds of the ten directions. At that time I received the Buddha's prediction, and later, at seventy-five, I shed this mortal frame and was reborn in Ultimate Bliss. Now, through my primal vow to benefit beings, I have returned to this world to teach and liberate in whatever ways suit each place.")

• The Records of Pure Land Sages and Worthies says: "From the 16th year of Chongzhen of the Ming to the 4th year of Shunzhi of the Qing, the Bodhisattva often manifested his spirit at Wu Gate to teach the Buddha-recitation Dharma-door."

• In the Precise Pointers to the West, the Bodhisattva teaches: "The mind is originally without thought; thought arises from imagination. That imagination is false, and keeps beings enduring samsara forever. Now you should know: this single phrase, A Di Đà Phật, is not born of imagination, does not come from thought, clings neither to inner nor outer, and has no marks at all. Understanding this clearly sweeps away all false thoughts; it is no different from the Buddha's Dharma-body, indistinguishable from it. To recite thus is to be free of affliction and worldly toil, unbroken, unabandoned — this is one-pointedness. Attaining this one-pointedness is called 'holding the name'; it is called 'one mind unconfused.'

*If in reciting the Buddha's name you lack one-pointedness, resolve to cut off wandering thoughts and recite slowly, so that voice accords with mind and mind accords with voice. Recite on and on like this; after a while wandering thoughts will settle, mind and surroundings will grow lucid, and you will realize Buddha-recitation samadhi. A verse says:

Speak little, one idle tale;

Recite much, one Buddha's name.

Strike wandering thoughts dead,

And vow your Dharma-body shall live.

Before reciting the Buddha's name, give rise to the great vow of rebirth in Ultimate Bliss; then with utter sincerity and earnestness call Amitabha's holy name. In reciting, let the voice follow the mind and the mind follow the voice, mind and voice supporting each other, held firm and never lost — and you will enter the samadhi of right recollection.

• In general, cultivators of pure karma, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, should face west — then stimulus and response come easily, and faculties and surroundings ripen readily. In one's hut, keep only one Buddha image, one sutra, and one incense burner; of tables, chairs, and bed, only one of each — nothing else should be kept. The courtyard too must be swept clean, so that walking meditation meets no obstacle. The essential point is to keep the mind unstained by a speck of dust, cut off ten thousand cares, open and lucid, unaware of body or of worldly life, unaware even that today's activity is cultivation. Thus one draws daily nearer the Path and farther from the world, and can turn toward pure karma.

The Pure Land method of cultivation lies in just two words: "single-minded diligence." Single-minded means adding nothing else; diligent means wasting not a moment. And in the practice of recitation by name, each word and phrase must join mind and voice, admitting not a speck of worldly thought; in time it ripens, and rebirth in Ultimate Bliss is certain — seated on a jeweled lotus, ascended to the stage of non-retrogression.

The Aspiration Verse of Bodhisattva Cizhou

Buddhas of the ten directions, three times,

Amitabha foremost,

Through nine grades liberating beings,

Majesty boundless.

Now I take full refuge,

Repenting the karma of the three deeds.

Whatever blessings I have,

I wholly dedicate.

May fellow cultivators all,

Respond in kind, appearing in time;

At life's end, the Buddha's realm

Manifesting clear before their eyes.

May all who see and hear grow diligent,

Together reborn in Ultimate Bliss,

Beholding the Buddha, freed from birth and death,

As the Buddha liberates all kinds.

---o0o---

tom_tat: (The Great Master, surnamed Jia, was a native of Yanmen, well versed in Confucian and Taoist teachings. At twenty-one, hearing Master Dao'an lecture on the Prajna sutras, he suddenly awakened and sighed: 'Confucian and Taoist studies are but chaff!' Thereupon he left home, vowing to spread the Buddha's teaching...)
noi_dung:
Great Master Huiyuan

(The Great Master, surnamed Jia, was a native of Yanmen, well versed in Confucian and Taoist teachings. At twenty-one, hearing Master Dao'an lecture on the Prajna sutras, he suddenly awakened and sighed: "Confucian and Taoist studies are but chaff!" Thereupon he left home, vowing to spread the Buddha's teaching. Master Hui'an once praised him: "Is it not through this Huiyuan that the true Dharma spreads in China?" Later the Great Master entered Mount Lu, where a dragon opened a spring for him and spirits moved timber to build Donglin Monastery. He dug a pond, planted lotuses, and gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha's name six times day and night, seeking rebirth in the West — hence the name Lotus Society. The Great Master remained in the mountains for more than thirty years; summoned by the emperor, he would not go. Three times he beheld the holy marks, yet in his humility he spoke of it to no one. In the 12th year of Yixi, the Buddha appeared again, and he sat upright and passed away, at eighty-three. Later generations honor the Great Master as the First Patriarch of the Lotus School.)

• The Great Master said: "What is Buddha-recitation samadhi? — It is exclusive recollection and tranquil contemplation. Exclusive recollection means the will undivided; tranquil contemplation means the breath pure and the spirit bright. With breath pure, wisdom-awareness shines everywhere; with spirit bright, it illumines the darkest places. These two subtly join and function together. Of the many named samadhis, in loftiness of merit and ease of progress, Buddha-recitation is foremost. Why? — Because the Tathagata is one who has perfectly realized the profound stillness of principle, in whom essence and spirit transform together, manifesting without end. Thus the cultivator of this meditation relies on the Buddha's power, and false awareness suddenly melts away; in the object contemplated, all grows still, like a bright mirror — the mirror of the mind bright, spiritual light interfusing, the myriad images displayed. Then seeing and hearing interpenetrate, no longer confined within ear and eye; the spiritual essence of one hue, naturally luminous. And the mind then accords with the profound principle, false sentiments melted away — what excellence in this world could surpass it?

I earnestly hope that all worthy ones cultivating this Dharma will strive in practice until awakening is joined — mindful that an inch of shadow swiftly fades, fearing merit still unfulfilled, sitting upright on the meditation cushion, cleansing the heart upon the Dharma seat, diligent by day, forgetting sleep by night. Only thus may you hope to walk with those above and guide those below."

---o0o---

tom_tat: (The Great Master was a native of Yanmen. As a boy roaming Mount Wutai, he was moved by miraculous signs to leave home. Fond of longevity arts, he once received ten volumes of immortals' scriptures from Tao Hongjing. Later meeting Bodhiruci, the Great Master asked: 'Does Buddhism have an art of longevity?'...)
noi_dung:
Great Master Tanluan

(The Great Master was a native of Yanmen. As a boy roaming Mount Wutai, he was moved by miraculous signs to leave home. Fond of longevity arts, he once received ten volumes of immortals' scriptures from Tao Hongjing. Later meeting Bodhiruci, the Great Master asked: "Does Buddhism have an art of longevity?" Bodhiruci handed him the Sutra of Sixteen Contemplations, saying: "This is Buddhism's art of longevity." The Great Master rejoiced, burned the immortals' scriptures, and devoted himself to pure karma — even in sickness, never resting for a moment. The Wei ruler, hearing his fame, honored him with the title Divine Luan. At life's end, the Great Master called the assembly and taught: "The sea of worldly toil and suffering — where is the shore of rest? The realms of hell are truly fearful; the Pure Land door must be cultivated." Speaking thus, he had the assembly loudly recite the Buddha's name, bowed toward the West, and passed away. At that moment all heard heavenly music sounding from the West, fading only after a long while.)

• The Great Master taught: "Beyond the primal vow of seeking rebirth, one must further give rise to the mind of enlightenment; whether rebirth is attained or not takes this as its ground."

• What is "ten thoughts in succession"? — Answer: It is like a man in an empty field, pursued by bandits with drawn swords bent on killing him. Terrified, he runs straight ahead until he reaches a river. Arriving, he thinks fleetingly: "If I can cross this river, I may yet save my life — but shall I swim across clothed, or strip first? If clothed, I fear the wide river will entangle me and I cannot get across; to strip takes time, and my pursuers are nearly upon me!" At that moment the man has but one thought — finding a means to cross — with absolutely no other idea. The Buddha-reciter is just the same: only earnest recitation, with no stray thoughts, mind following mind for ten thoughts — this is called "ten thoughts in succession."

• Those who recite the Buddha's name should in ordinary times agree with five or three fellow cultivators to remind and assist one another in recitation at life's end. Then rebirth will be firmly assured.

---o0o---

tom_tat: (The Great Master, named Zhi Kai, was the founding patriarch of the Tiantai school. Surnamed Chen, a native of Yongchuan, at his birth a spirit-light shone throughout the house. At eighteen he left home and studied under Meditation Master Huisi. Seeing him arrive, the meditation master said: 'Long ago you and I were together in the Vulture Peak assembly; past affinities pursue us, and now we meet again...')
noi_dung:
Great Master Zhizhe

(The Great Master, named Zhi Kai, was the founding patriarch of the Tiantai school. Surnamed Chen, a native of Yongchuan, at his birth a spirit-light shone throughout the house. At eighteen he left home and studied under Meditation Master Huisi. Seeing him arrive, the meditation master said: "Long ago you and I were together in the Vulture Peak assembly; past affinities pursue us, and now we meet again." The Great Master followed Huisi, cultivating single-mindedly, and before long realized Lotus samadhi, his wisdom and eloquence unobstructed. He composed the Ten Doubts on the Pure Land to urge people to recite the Buddha's name. Emperor Xuan of Chen, admiring his virtue, built a monastery and invited the Great Master to preside. Emperor Yang of Sui also took the precepts under him and bestowed the title Zhizhe, the Wise One. Later the Great Master returned to Mount Tiantai, where his teaching flourished ever more. In winter of the 17th year of Kaihuang, facing west, he recited the Buddha's name and passed away seated, at sixty-seven.)

• The Great Master said: "To be certain of rebirth in the West, two practices are needed: Renunciation and Joyful Aspiration.

What is the practice of Renunciation? Contemplate this body as full of impurity, enduring many pains, with nothing joyful in it — and give rise to weariness, wishing to escape. Reflecting thus, the fires of lust and affliction gradually lessen. Further vow to be forever parted from this dusty realm of suffering and toil, to receive no more a male or female body of blood and pus, foul-smelling, intoxicated by the five desires — seeking swift rebirth in the Pure Land to realize the pure, radiant Dharma-nature body. This is the practice of Renunciation.

What is the practice of Joyful Aspiration? Here there are two points:

1. Reflect that beings are drowning in the sea of suffering, while you are an ordinary mortal powerless to save them. Now you earnestly wish to reach Ultimate Bliss, draw near the Buddha, cultivate until the unborn is realized — liberating yourself, repaying the four kindnesses, and rescuing suffering beings. This is the aim of seeking rebirth.

2. Picture in mind the Buddha's reward body, golden and radiant, with 84,000 marks, each mark with 84,000 beauties, each beauty emitting 84,000 rays of light, shining throughout the Dharma-realm and gathering in all who recite the Buddha's name. Further contemplate Ultimate Bliss adorned with seven jewels, replete with wondrous bliss, and give rise to delight. Hence practice giving, keep the precepts, recite the Buddha's name, cultivate all wholesome deeds, then dedicate them, vowing that you and all beings alike be reborn in the Pure Land. Acting thus, rebirth is certain — and this is the practice of Joyful Aspiration.

---o0o---

tom_tat: The Great Master, surnamed Wei, was a native of Tinh Chau. At fourteen he left home, studied the sutras and treatises, and also followed Meditation Master Toan in Chan practice. Later, dwelling at Huyen Trang Monastery in the Bich Coc valley, he admired the pure-karma practice of Dharma Master Tanluan and constantly bowed and recited, six times daily, seated in stillness facing west...
noi_dung:
Great Master Daochuo

The Great Master, surnamed Wei, was a native of Tinh Chau. At fourteen he left home, studied the sutras and treatises, and also followed Meditation Master Toan in Chan practice. Later, dwelling at Huyen Trang Monastery in the Bich Coc valley, he admired the pure-karma practice of Dharma Master Tanluan and constantly bowed and recited, six times daily, seated in stillness facing west. The Great Master set himself a daily quota of seventy thousand Buddha-recitations. A monk in meditation saw him holding a rosary radiant as a mountain of seven jewels. Other miraculous signs are beyond counting. The Great Master lectured on the three Pure Land sutras nearly two hundred times; when each lecture ended, the assembly scattered to recite the Buddha's name, their voices ringing through forests and mountains. Even in nearby districts, children of seven and up all knew to recite the Buddha's name. When the Master reached life's end, the assembly saw a manifested Buddha in the sky and heavenly flowers raining down — and looking again, he had already passed away.

• The Great Master said: "Cultivators of pure karma, whether sitting or lying down, must never turn their backs to the West, nor spit or relieve themselves facing west. Having taken refuge in the lotus land, one should revere that golden realm; without a reverent heart, where is the resolve to seek rebirth?"

• Question: Reciting Amitabha's red name can erase the karma of dark ignorance and win rebirth — yet some recite while ignorance remains and their wish is unfulfilled. What is the reason? Answer: Because they do not cultivate in accord with truth, and their practice does not match the Name's meaning — for they do not know the Tathagata as the true-mark body, the body that is Buddha. There are also three kinds of non-correspondence, and hence no rebirth.

1. Faith impure — now present, now absent.

2. Faith not single — ever changing, never resolved.

3. Faith not sustained — constantly broken off by stray thoughts.

Thus in reciting the Buddha's name, gather the mind and let it not scatter; recitation sustained is faith, is one-pointedness, is purity of heart. To recite thus and yet not be reborn — that would be against all reason.

---o0o---

tom_tat: The Great Master was the Second Patriarch of the Lotus School. At first, seeing Master Daochuo's pure-karma practice center, he rejoiced, saying: 'Here at last is the secret path to Buddhahood.' He then went to the capital to exhort the assembly in Pure Land practice, often kneeling to recite the Buddha's name until his strength gave out...
noi_dung:
Great Master Shandao

The Great Master was the Second Patriarch of the Lotus School. At first, seeing Master Daochuo's pure-karma practice center, he rejoiced, saying: "Here at last is the secret path to Buddhahood." He then went to the capital to exhort the assembly in Pure Land practice, often kneeling to recite the Buddha's name until his strength gave out. The Great Master taught the Pure Land door for more than thirty years, cultivating diligently, never once sleeping. Whatever offerings he received he used to copy the Amitabha Sutra — more than a hundred thousand copies — and to paint the holy scenes of the West — more than three hundred pictures. The Great Master transformed a vast multitude of monastics and laity, among whom those who attained samadhi and rebirth in the Pure Land are beyond counting. One day he climbed a willow tree, faced west, made his vow, then cast himself down — falling lightly as a leaf — and passed away seated in full lotus. Emperor Gaozong honored his shrine and named his monastery Radiant Light.

• The Great Master taught: "The great sages, in compassion, urge people to single-mindedly call the Name, because calling the Name is most easy: if each thought can follow the next, taking the whole life as one's practice, then of ten who cultivate, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred. Why? Because with no mixed affinities, right mindfulness is attained; because it accords with the Buddha's primal vow; because it does not contradict the sutras; because it follows the Buddha's words. To abandon singleness for mixed practice — of a hundred, perhaps one or two; of a thousand, three or four at most will be reborn."

• Those who recite the Buddha's name should not fear death at life's end. Reflect often: this body is impure and endures much suffering — to cast off this illusory body and be reborn in the Pure Land is truly cause for joy!

• In sickness, think only of impermanence and single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name awaiting death. Instruct those close to you: when visitors come, urge them to recite the Buddha's name for you — no idle worldly talk. If gravely ill and near death, those around must not weep; all should recite the Buddha's name together and wait until the sick person's body has grown wholly cold before attending to anything else. To have someone versed in the Pure Land teaching come often to encourage and remind you — that is truly great good fortune. Following this method, rebirth is certain.

• The matter of life, death, and revolving rebirth is immense; you must exert yourself to succeed — if a single thought goes astray and the moment is wasted, many kalpas of suffering follow, and who can take your place? Reflect carefully, reflect carefully.

• Before retiring, bow to the Buddha, contemplate, then read this vow: "I... am an ordinary mortal amid birth and death, my karmic obstacles heavy and deep, revolving through the six paths, my suffering beyond words! Now meeting a wise teacher, I have heard the holy name of Amitabha Buddha, with that Buddha's primal vows and merits; with one heart I call his name, seeking rebirth. May the Buddha in compassion not abandon me but pity and embrace me. Now your disciple does not yet know the Buddha's body, his beautiful marks and radiance — may the Buddha manifest them that I may see. Nor do I yet know Avalokiteshvara, Mahasthamaprapta, the Bodhisattva assembly, their wondrous radiant marks, and that world's pure adornments — may you let me see them clearly."

• Before sleep, contemplate the sublime scenes of the West, or the Buddha's fine marks — no idle talk, no craving for auspicious signs, only single-minded cultivation, and in time you will see. Or simply recite the Buddha's name until you fall asleep. In the above, take one method alone, without mixing. And it must be practiced steadily and long — then pure-karma effort will never be in vain.

---o0o---

tom_tat: (Of his origins, little is known. It is known only that at first, together with Masters Xuanzang and Ci'en, he belonged to the Dharma-Marks school. Stern and resolute by nature, austere and diligent in study, he doubted: 'Reciting the Buddha's name for so short a time — how can one be reborn in the West?'...)
noi_dung:
Great Master Huaigan

(Of his origins, little is known. It is known only that at first, together with Masters Xuanzang and Ci'en, he belonged to the Dharma-Marks school. Stern and resolute by nature, austere and diligent in study, he doubted: "Reciting the Buddha's name for so short a time — how can one be reborn in the West?" and brought this question to Patriarch Shandao. The Patriarch said: "Those are the Buddha's truthful words — could they be false?" And he told him to enter the recitation hall and seek proof in practice. The Great Master obeyed, cultivating twenty-one days with no auspicious sign; hating his own deep obstacles, he wished to starve himself to death. The Patriarch forbade it and urged him to continue. He cultivated with vigor for three years, until the Buddha emitted golden light and he beheld the white-curl mark — realizing Buddha-recitation samadhi. Thereupon he wrote the seven-volume Treatise Resolving the Many Doubts on the Pure Land. At life's end, the Great Master saw a manifested Buddha come to receive him, and facing west, passed away.)

• The Great Master taught: "Mindful recitation with whole heart is the karma of the will doing good; calling the Buddha's name is the karma of the mouth doing good; joining palms in worship is the karma of the body doing good. Through these three karmas of goodness, one can erase the grave offenses of birth and death through eighty million kalpas, and — practice and vow supporting each other — rebirth is certain."

• One should recite the Buddha's name aloud — samadhi comes easily so; silent recitation mostly scatters the mind. This practitioners know in themselves; outsiders cannot fathom it.

• The method of reciting in a dark room is nowhere mentioned in the sacred teachings. Yet beginners, in a dark room — cut off from all seeing and hearing, casting off all ties, single-mindedly reciting — will find samadhi comes easily. It is like worldly people wrestling with a hard problem they cannot solve, because of scattered thoughts: shutting the door, sitting alone, eyes closed, the mind grows calm, and gradually a thread of solution appears. Those who have never practiced will doubt this; to those who have, it is an essential point.

Editor's note: The Third, Fourth, and Fifth Patriarchs of the Lotus School — Masters Chengyuan, Fazhao, and Shaokang — taught and transformed beings most flourishingly, but their teachings were lost; only their life stories remain. As for the Fourth Patriarch Fazhao, the popular "Five-Tone Recitation" is not acknowledged by Great Master Yinguang, who deems it a later fabrication. To keep only the essence and spare the reader excess, it is not translated here.

---o0o---

While still serving in office, he used tax money to buy living creatures and release them, and was sentenced to death — yet his expression never changed, so the king pardoned him. Afterward he left home, first studying under Chan Master Cuiyan, then training with National Teacher Shao, gaining wisdom and eloquence when Avalokiteshvara sprinkled sweet dew upon his mouth...)
noi_dung:
Great Master Yongming

(He was the Sixth Patriarch of the Lotus School, lay surname Wang, a native of Tien Duong. While still serving in office, he used tax money to buy living creatures and release them, and was sentenced to death — yet his expression never changed, so the king pardoned him. Afterward he left home, first studying under Chan Master Cuiyan, then training with National Teacher Shao, gaining wisdom and eloquence when Avalokiteshvara sprinkled sweet dew upon his mouth. The Great Master authored the one-hundred-volume Mirror of the Source and the Collection on Ten Thousand Goods Returning to the Same, urging Pure Land practice. King Zhongyi, admiring his virtue, invited him to preside at Yongming Monastery. The Great Master set himself 108 good deeds daily; at night he climbed the peak to recite the Buddha's name, and people heard heavenly music resounding in the sky. He recited the Lotus Sutra to a total of thirteen thousand copies. In the 8th year of Kaibao, the Great Master burned incense, bade the assembly farewell, and passed away seated, at seventy-two.)

• The Great Master taught: "Take refuge with one heart, cultivate with vigor all your life; sitting or lying, ever face west. In worshiping, reciting, and vowing, be earnest and utterly sincere, admitting no stray thought — as one under torture, as one in prison, as one pursued by vengeful foes, as one pressed by flood and fire — single-heartedly crying for rescue, vowing to escape the wheel of suffering and swiftly realize the unborn, to continue the Three Jewels, repay the four kindnesses, and liberate all that breathes. Such sincerity never labors in vain. But if words and deeds disagree, faith unsteady, recitation ever broken and unsustained — to hope for rebirth with such laziness, I fear that at life's end good friends will be hard to meet, karma will drag you down, pain will crush you, and right mindfulness will not form. Why? The present is the cause, life's end the fruit: only a true cause yields an unspoiled fruit — as a loud sound carries its echo far, as a straight form casts a straight shadow.

• Joyful and painful retribution are both made by the mind. A mind of anger and lust is hell-karma; a mind of greedy miserliness is hungry-ghost karma; a mind of deluded darkness is animal karma; a mind of arrogant pride is asura karma; keeping the five precepts in full is human karma; perfecting the ten wholesome deeds is heavenly karma; realizing the emptiness of persons is Hearer karma; understanding the emptiness of conditioned arising is Solitary-Realizer karma; practicing the six perfections is Bodhisattva karma; a truly equal compassionate heart is Buddha-karma. If the mind is pure, one is born transformed in the Pure Land, in jeweled pavilions and fragrant towers; if the mind is defiled, one lodges one's substance in a filthy land, among hills, pits, and ditches. Myriad realms are all made by mind — apart from the mind-source there are no forms at all. To reap wholesome fruit, cultivate pure causes.

• The Four Choices in verse say:

With Chan, without Pure Land,

Ten seekers, nine miss the road.

When the bardo realms appear,

In a blink they follow karma.

Without Chan, with Pure Land,

Ten thousand cultivators, ten thousand reborn.

Beholding Amitabha,

What fear of not awakening?

With Chan, with Pure Land,

Like a tiger grown with horns.

This life a teacher of people,

Next life a Buddha, a Patriarch.

Without Chan, without Pure Land —

Iron beds, bronze pillars of fire.

Ten thousand kalpas, a thousand lives,

With no refuge anywhere!

Editor's note: Master Xingchang, Seventh Patriarch of the Lotus School — his teaching was lost to transmission; only his life story remains, so it is not given here.

noi_dung:
Great Master Zunshi

(The Master, surnamed Diep, was a native of Thai Chau, born after his mother prayed to Avalokiteshvara. He received the full precepts at twenty, first studying the vinaya, then entering Quoc Thanh Monastery to train in the Tiantai contemplations. The Great Master bent his whole will on rebirth in Ultimate Bliss, cultivating the Pratyutpanna samadhi with such austerity that he vomited blood. With firm resolve, he made death his deadline and never rested. One night in a dream he saw Avalokiteshvara point at his mouth and draw out several worms; from the Bodhisattva's fingertip sweet dew streamed into his throat, and his sickness was cured. Later, at Bao Yun Monastery, he led the assembly in pure-karma cultivation together. The Great Master authored the Amitabha Repentance Rite, Resolving Doubts on the Pure Land, the Ten-Recitations Method, and Brief Biographies of the Reborn — all circulating in the world. At life's end, he burned incense, bowed to the Three Jewels seeking witness, and recited the Buddha's name as he passed, at sixty-nine.)

*The Great Master said: — Cultivators of pure karma, whatever work they do, though passing through many tangled ties, must never in mind forget the Buddha-recitation. It is like worldly people with some pressing matter unresolved: meeting other ties, coming and going, sitting and rising, talking and laughing, bustling through this and that — yet their minds never stop turning over the earlier matter. The reciter's mindfulness must be trained just the same; when recitation slips away, gather it back — in time it becomes habit, and recollection grows free. Hence the Shurangama Sutra says: "Gathering the mind thus, one can naturally check evil thoughts. Even wishing to do evil, through remembering the Buddha the evil cannot be done — as one whose body carries fragrance naturally dispels all stench."

• Rising early, dressed, join palms toward the West and recite the Buddha's name. Take a long breath and recite continuously through its whole length — this counts as one thought; ten such breaths are ten thoughts. But do not strain: long or short of breath, high or low of voice, slow or quick — all as your strength allows. Done, make a brief vow seeking rebirth in the West. If you keep a Buddha image, recite before it, bowing three times on entering and on leaving. This ten-recitations method is most convenient for those with many ties. Practiced truly each day, with the whole life as its term, rebirth is certain.

---o0o---

noi_dung:
Great Master Cijue

(The Great Master, named Tong Trach, was a native of Tuong Duong. He left home under Chan Master Tu at Truong Lo Monastery, awakening to the mind's essence. In the Nguyen Huu years, the Great Master brought his aged mother to live in the eastern abbot's quarters and urged her to recite the Buddha's name. Seven years later she was reborn in the Pure Land. Following the rule of Mount Lu, he founded the Superior Lotus Assembly, urging monks and laity to recite the Buddha's name — and the two Bodhisattvas Samantabhadra and Samantawisdom appeared in dreams asking to enroll, showing their secret guardianship and assent. From then on, followers flocked to him in ever greater numbers. Vinaya Master Lingzhi praised him as the Mahayana teacher of that age. At life's end, he passed away seated in full lotus, reciting the Buddha's name.)

• The Great Master said: — Beginners on the Path, whose forbearance is not yet pure, must borrow pure conditions to aid their progress. Why? — Because in this Saha world Shakyamuni Buddha has entered extinction and Maitreya has not yet descended; while in Ultimate Bliss, kind father Amitabha is even now teaching. Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta — people of Saha thirst in vain for their fair names, but in the Pure Land those superior good persons are one's close friends. — In Saha, hosts of demons rise to trouble cultivators; but in Ultimate Bliss, within the great radiance, what demonic deeds could remain? — In Saha, deviant voices easily confuse and beauty beguiles the heart; in Ultimate Bliss, birds, waters, forests and trees all proclaim the wondrous Dharma, the reward-body pure, and there are no women! Cultivation conditions, complete and favorable, are nowhere greater than in the West — a pity that shallow, weak-faith folk doubt and slander instead! Let me set out a few points for discussion:

+ In this world, the noisy household life wearies people, so many love the lonely temple and leave home. But Saha's sufferings are not only household afflictions, and Ultimate Bliss's joys, wondrous beyond measure, are not merely temple quietude! To know leaving home is good yet refuse to seek rebirth — this is the first error.

+ In this world, cultivators toil painfully, traveling ten thousand miles to find a wise teacher who can clarify the great matter and settle birth-and-death samsara. In Ultimate Bliss, Amitabha, World-Honored One — form, mind, and vow-power all supreme — need only sound the perfect voice, and all who hear awaken. To wish to consult wise teachers yet not wish to behold the Buddha is the second error. In this world, cultivators seeing a great monastery with a large assembly all delight and wish to stay, shunning places with few members. In Ultimate Bliss, those of One Birth More are a great multitude; superior good persons gather in one place. To love great monasteries yet not cherish the pure ocean-wide assembly of the West is the third error.

+ In this world, even the long-lived pass not a hundred years — and reckon: foolish childhood, feeble old age, sickness, sleep — these alone consume more than half a life. Besides, even Bodhisattvas grow dim at the barrier between lives, even Hearers are veiled at emergence from the womb; an inch of shadow worth a thousand gold is nine-tenths spent, yet cultivation has not reached non-retrogression — truly chilling to the heart! In the West, life is immeasurable: once one's substance is entrusted to the lotus, there is no more suffering of birth, age, sickness, death — cultivation continues unbroken until enlightenment is realized. To willingly revolve in short, bitter Saha and forget long-spring Ultimate Bliss is the fourth error.

+ In this world, only those who have realized the unborn — dwelling amid desires yet unstained — may wield compassion and skillful wisdom to rescue all kinds. But those of shallow wisdom, touching a little goodness, deem themselves lofty and free, scorn the Pure Land, cling to Saha, unmeasured against great-power Bodhisattvas — and one day must fall revolving. This is the fifth error. The sutra says: "You should vow rebirth in that land" — yet some disbelieve the Buddha's words and despise seeking rebirth. Is this not delusion? Alas! Those who do not plan far will know near sorrow; once this body is lost, ten thousand kalpas of regret — then how to turn back in time!

---o0o---

noi_dung:
Great Master Cizhao

(The Master, named Tu Nguyen, styled Van Su Huu (All Matters Ended), surnamed Mau, was a native of Con Son. His mother dreamed of a Buddha entering the door, and bore him. At nineteen he left home, training in calming-and-insight, and awakened hearing a crow's cry. Deeply compassionate, the Great Master founded the White Lotus Repentance Hall and composed the White Lotus repentance rite, bowing to the Buddhas in repentance on beings' behalf, urging all to keep the precepts, recite the Buddha's name, and seek rebirth in the West. He further authored the "Perfect-and-Interpenetrating Four Lands, Three Contemplations, Selecting the Buddha Chart," revealing the Lotus School's guiding eye. Emperor Xiaozong summoned him to Duc Tho Hall to teach the Pure Land Dharma-door and bestowed the title White Lotus Guide. At life's end he passed away with palms joined; at the cremation, relics appeared beyond number.)

• The Great Master taught: "If you now wish to cultivate the Buddha-recitation samadhi and seek rebirth in the Pure Land so as swiftly to realize enlightenment, then the principal practice is single-minded Buddha-recitation. The supporting practices are to cut off evil, do good, and dedicate that merit toward the West. This is called floating with the downstream current while adding the oar — swiftly reaching the shore."

• Morning and evening, single-heartedly worship Amitabha Buddha as you would attend a king — never missing the appointed time; practiced long, intimacy grows. As for recitation: mouth reciting, mind imagining, mind and mouth joined, giving rise to a heart of grateful reverence, firm faith beyond doubt — day by day more ripe — and samadhi comes of itself.

• At life's end there are often three doubts and four barriers that obstruct rebirth; prepare by reflecting beforehand to dispel them. The three doubts are:

1) Doubting that one's past karma is deep and practice-time short, fearing rebirth cannot be won.

2) Doubting that one's vows are unpaid and greed, anger, and delusion unsevered, fearing rebirth cannot be won.

3) Doubting that in reciting, the Buddha may not come to receive one, fearing rebirth cannot be won.

The four barriers are:

1) Under sickness and pain, slandering the Buddha as powerless.

2) Clinging to life, killing creatures to offer in worship.

3) Taking medicines containing wine or bloody, fishy substances.

4) Bound by fond love, tying oneself to family.

A note: The Great Master set out the three doubts and four barriers but left no method for resolving them — for in olden times the faithful understood much and could reflect and guard themselves, or perhaps he did teach it and transmission was lost. In any case, for those of shallow faith and little understanding, these points pose no small danger. Here I venture to outline their refutation, from which readers may reflect and extend further.

Refuting the first doubt: Amitabha Buddha's primal vow declares that beings who wholeheartedly aspire to Ultimate Bliss and call his name even ten times, if not reborn there — then he vows not to become a Buddha. The Buddha never lies; practitioners must trust him. Ten thoughts are the briefest practice, yet even they win rebirth — how much more our greater recitation! Moreover, however heavy one's karmic obstacles, wholehearted faithful recitation at life's end surely wins rebirth. Of old, Truong Thien Hoa, who butchered oxen all his life, saw hell manifest at life's end; in terror he recited the Buddha's name, and at once saw the Buddha come to receive him. Even mynahs and parrots that recite are reborn — how much more ourselves, not yet so fallen!

Refuting the second doubt: The Milinda Sutra says: "A light grain of sand dropped in water sinks at once; yet a great heavy boulder, carried by boat, may be borne from place to place." Reciters are the same: trusting recitation wins rebirth however weighty one's karma — borne by the Buddha's vow-power, like the great boulder carried by boat, which cannot sink. Buddha-recitation is the Dharma of "rebirth with karma still borne" — so cultivators must not think greed, anger, and delusion still present bar rebirth in the West. This example refutes the heavy-karma doubt of the first point as well. As for vows, there are two kinds: religious and worldly.

Religiously, one may have vowed to build a temple or recite a number of sutras and mantras, unfulfilled when death comes. Reflect: faithful recitation alone wins rebirth; vows fulfilled or not do no harm. Worldly, one's family duties may be unfinished — aged parents above with none to care for them, or a young wife and children below with no support — the heart's wish unrounded, the mind uneasy. Reflect: now near death, worry or not, nothing can be done. Set it aside, recite with whole heart; once in the West with the fruit realized, all vows and tangled ties can be repaid, all debtors of love and enmity can be saved.

Refuting the third doubt: Through the Buddha's primal vow and one's own merit, at life's end a Buddha, Bodhisattva, or holy host will surely come to receive the reciter — the essential point is then to contemplate the Buddha wholeheartedly and think of nothing else; doubt itself breeds obstruction. In short, at life's end, whether auspicious signs appear or not, pay them no heed — only recite with full heart to the very last moment.

Refuting the four barriers together: Sickness befalling a reciter comes from cultivation's merit, turning heavy future retribution into light present retribution — repaid in full so as to win rebirth. To doubt and slander instead marks shallow faith, betraying the Buddha's kindness and heaping karmic obstruction on oneself. Of old, Ngo Mao cultivated truly; caught in rebellion, he was pierced by seven spears and died. When his brother came, he suddenly revived and said: "For past grave offenses I should have fallen at death — but through this life's vegetarian diet, recitation, and good deeds, the heavy fruit was lightened: I must bear these seven wounds to repay seven future lives as a pig. Now the Buddha receives me into the West." From this one tale the rest may be inferred. This body is provisional — according to past offenses and blessings its lifespan holds joy or pain, long or short. Knowing vegetarian diet, precepts, and recitation, trust the Buddha utterly and trust cause and effect with certainty. In sickness or at life's end, only repent and recite. Never invite sorcerers or mediums, kill creatures in offering, or — heeding the ignorant — return to meat and wine or medicines of bloody, fishy stuff. And within the family — parents, siblings, spouses, children — all gather briefly through past debts of love and enmity; when ties end, each goes their way. Shake off worldly feeling, seek rebirth in the West to liberate all debtors of love and enmity. When death comes, clinging accompanies nothing and avails nothing — only revolving rebirth, no rebirth in the Pure Land. Reflect and remember well.

Thich Thien Tam

---o0o---
