noi_dung:
Great Master Youyan

(The Master, surnamed Ho, was a native of Lam Hai. At six he left home at Linh Thuu Monastery; at fourteen he received the full precepts. Studying under Dharma Master Than Chieu, he awakened to the meaning of the One Mind's Three Contemplations. He then became lecturer at Xich Thanh Monastery, later dwelling in seclusion on the eastern peak of Co Son; beside his hut stood a tra tree, and he styled himself Tra Hermitage. The Great Master kept the vinaya most strictly, owning nothing beyond robe and bowl. He devoted himself to pure karma, attaining samadhi with many miraculous responses; whatever he wrote proclaimed the Lotus School. In the first year of Tinh Quoc, one day he saw a deva descend from the sky saying: "Your pure karma is accomplished!" The Great Master further dreamed of a great lotus blooming in a pond amid heavenly music; waking, he composed a verse to bid himself farewell. Seven days later he passed away seated upright.)

*The Great Master said: — The World-Honored One in pity uses many expedients to receive sentient beings. Thus those who win rebirth do so in many ways: through meditative or scattered goodness, through the Buddha's power or the Dharma's power; some cultivate blessings alone and borrow vow-power to dedicate; some at life's end, terrified, recite and are saved. Such kinds number in the thousands — yet relying on a single method, rebirth is won. As to meditative goodness: those cultivating wondrous contemplation, the Shurangama samadhi. As to scattered goodness: the Sutra of Immeasurable Life says, "With ten thoughts reciting the Buddha, rebirth is likewise won." As to the Buddha's power: through Amitabha's great compassionate vow-power embracing them, reciting beings rely on it to be reborn — as a common man riding with a wheel-turning king may circle the four continents in a day and night, not by his own power but by the Wheel King's might. As to the Dharma's power: as when the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Lotus-Radiance Vidyaraja to empower sand with mantra and scatter it on the corpses or graves of the dead, so that the departed — though fallen among hells, hungry ghosts, or animals — relying on this true word, reach Ultimate Bliss. As to dedicating cultivated blessings: keeping a compassionate heart that harms no life, keeping the precepts, reciting secret mantras and Mahayana scriptures, and cultivating blessings, dedicated to adorn the Pure Land cause. As to crying for rescue in terror at life's end: at death's approach the fire-chariot appears; calling the Buddha's name, raging fire turns to cool breeze — as with Hung Tuan and Truong Thien Hoa, who were reborn.

---o0o---

Under the Yuan dynasty, in the first year of Dai Chi, the White Lotus sect flourished so that true and false could not be told apart, and the king ordered the Lotus School abolished...)
noi_dung:
Great Master Youtan

(The Great Master, named Pho Do, surnamed Tuong, was a native of Don Duong. He left home at Dong Lam Monastery on Mount Lu, devoted to the Pure Land. Under the Yuan dynasty, in the first year of Dai Chi, the White Lotus sect flourished so that true and false could not be told apart, and the king ordered the Lotus School abolished. The Great Master said: "I have cultivated the Pure Land nearly thirty years — shall this Dharma-door perish in my own lifetime?" He wrote the ten-volume Precious Mirror of the Lotus School and invited great virtues of all quarters to witness it — none could alter a word. Then, presenting it overnight for the king's review, he won praise and an order to carve the blocks for circulation. The king further bestowed the title Venerable Tiger Brook and made him hierarch of the Lotus School. At life's end he passed away reciting the Buddha's name.)

*The Great Master taught: — Cultivators of pure karma, if worldly dust is not yet cleansed, when evil thoughts arise must loudly recite the Buddha's name to gather into right mindfulness — never let evil minds continue. Know that today's cultivation is open battle with birth-and-death karma, no common matter; ever mindful of swift impermanence — days and months wait for none — take up the true and real and recite. Half advancing, half retreating, now believing, now doubting — in the end pure karma is unaccomplished; how to escape samsara?

• Hold one phrase of the Buddha's name as you would lean on Mount Sumeru — unshakable; ever mindful, ever reciting: morning reciting, evening reciting, walking reciting, sitting reciting, the mindful heart never forsaking, the Buddha's name never leaving the heart, each moment never parted — thought upon thought, as a hen brooding eggs keeps the warmth unbroken. This is called "pure mindfulness in succession."

• To be reborn in the Pure Land, reflect that all worldly things are impermanent: what forms must break, what lives must die. Had we never heard the Buddha's teaching, we would shed this body for another, drifting through the three realms and six paths, none knowing when to escape. Now blessed to hear the true teaching and cultivate pure karma, single-minded recitation means that casting off this body we enter a lotus womb in the Buddha's land, enjoy every bliss, escape all suffering utterly, and go straight to the enlightenment path — the lifelong resolve of a great hero.

• At the first onset of sickness, vigorously cast off ten thousand ties, sit upright facing west, picture Amitabha, Avalokiteshvara, Mahasthamaprapta, and manifested Buddhas all before you, and wholeheartedly call the Buddha's name, each call unbroken upon the next. Then think nothing of worldly affairs; should such a thought flash up, swiftly call the Buddha's name — in each thought offenses are erased; this single thought surely wins rebirth. If your lifespan is not yet ended, you will naturally recover. Beware of vainly clinging to the world: this body — kept if kept, lost if lost — seek only rebirth, doubting and caring for nothing else. Understand: even to die is as one casting off ragged clothes to don fine garments — shedding a mortal body to ascend to the Buddha's land. Is this not joy?

• Single the mind's will and hold one phrase, A Di Đà Phật: this one thought alone is my fundamental teacher; this one thought before me, a manifested Buddha; this one thought, a fierce general smashing hell; this one thought, a jeweled sword cutting down deviant hosts; this one thought, a bright torch shattering darkness; this one thought, a great ship crossing the sea of suffering; this one thought, wondrous medicine curing birth-and-death sickness; this one thought, the shortcut out of the three realms; this one thought, the self-nature Amitabha; this one thought, the mind-only Pure Land. Only hold fast this recitation and let it never be lost: each thought ever present, each thought never parted from mind — idle, recite thus; busy, recite thus; joyful, recite thus; sick and suffering, recite thus; living, recite thus; dying, recite thus. Holding one thought clear like this — what need to ask another the way home?

---o0o---

noi_dung:
Great Master Tianru

(The Master, surnamed Dam, named Duy Tac, was a native of Vinh Hung. He received the Dharma from Chan Master Trung Phong Minh Ban. In the first year of Chi Chanh, the Great Master presided at Su Tu Lam Monastery in To Chau. The ministers and elders of that age mostly came to study under him. The king often sent edicts inviting him, but he always declined on grounds of sickness. The Great Master had secretly joined the Chan essence while also spreading Pure Land teaching, once writing the "Questions and Doubts on the Pure Land" to shatter doubts and urge recitation for rebirth in the West. He cultivated most diligently, passing away in the first year of Hongwu of the Ming, with many auspicious signs at his passing, at seventy-one.)

• Someone asked: — The perfect-contemplation practice and the mind-only recitation method seem to be doors for those of superior faculties. And the ten vows of the Avatamsaka Sutra, the ten resolves of the Ratnakuta Sutra, are likewise the workings of great wisdom. On the path, if faculties and teaching do not match, I fear practice can hardly succeed. Examining my own nature, I should only hold singlemindedly to the Name, with added worship and repentance — what is your honored view?

The Great Master replied: — Excellent! One who knows their own measure! Your words accord with Master Shandao's teaching of Exclusive Uninterrupted Cultivation. Uninterrupted Cultivation means: the body worships Amitabha Buddha alone, no other; the mouth calls Amitabha's name alone, no other; the mind contemplates Amitabha Buddha alone, no other.

• In reciting, some contemplate the thirty-two marks, binding the mind to steadiness until, eyes open or closed, the Buddha is seen. Others single-mindedly call the Name, guarding against scattering, and likewise behold him in this very life. Of these two, for beholding the Buddha, the Name-calling method is mostly superior. Name-calling requires binding the heart against scattering, each thought succeeding the next, following the Buddha's name, each phrase, each word distinct. And in calling the Buddha's name, never mind much or little — one heart, one mind, thought upon thought in succession. Only thus are the grave offenses of birth and death through eighty million kalpas erased; otherwise, erasing offenses is most hard.

• Someone asked: — A life of evil, yet at life's end ten thoughts still win rebirth. Then may I now follow worldly ties and wait until death approaches to recite — would that do?

• The Great Master replied: — How bitter! These words harm yourself and harm monks, nuns, men, and women of the age besides! Know that wicked mortals who recite at life's end and are saved do so through past-life roots of goodness, meeting a wise teacher's guidance — a one-in-ten-thousand chance. The Treatise on Groups of Doubts speaks of "ten kinds who at life's end cannot recite: 1) hardly meeting a good friend, with none to urge recitation; 2) sickness binding the body, no leisure to recite; 3) apoplexy locking the throat, no voice to speak; 4) madness losing all clarity; 5) sudden calamity of water or fire; 6) seized and devoured by tigers or wolves; 7) evil friends destroying faith; 8) dying in stupor; 9) sudden death amid battle; 10) falling from a high place." These occur constantly in life, drawn by past or present karma, striking suddenly beyond all escape. Meeting one such hapless stroke among the ten — how could you recite? Suppose none of these evil ties befall you and you die of a light illness — still I fear that at life's end, as the four elements part, pain like knife-cuts, like a crab dropped in boiling water — amid such tormenting anguish, panicked and bewildered, what leisure to recite? Suppose you die without sickness — still I fear worldly ties unsevered, vulgar thoughts unforgotten, clinging to life, fearing death, the heart tangled and uneasy. Add a household unordered, after-matters unarranged, wife and children wailing and calling, a hundred threads of fear and grief — how then to recite? Suppose before death comes sickness — then groaning pain, seeking doctors and remedies, urgent rites and offerings, a tangle of scattered thoughts — can recitation prevail? Suppose before sickness comes age — then the suffering of years, dotage and trembling, gloom and despair — fretting over this aging body unfinished, what leisure to recite? Suppose before age, still young and strong — yet if soaring ambitions unquelled and worldly ties still bind, rushing east and west, scheming this and that, consciousness dreaming — still no recitation! Suppose blessed with idle leisure and a cultivating will — yet without seeing through life as false dream, the body at rest but the mind still tangled, unable to cast off ten thousand ties; when matters come, self-mastery lost, deranged by circumstances — still no recitation! Consider: not to speak of age and sickness — even in youthful leisure, if one matter clings to the heart, recitation already fails. How much less waiting for life's end? To be upright in mindfulness at death and be reborn, you must right now see worldly affairs as illusory dreams, accord with conditions and pass the days in contentment, cling no more; whenever idle, recite; never delay putting it off or waste the hours. Thus provisions prepared in advance, nothing obstructs the departure.

---o0o---

noi_dung:
Great Master Miaoxie

(The Great Master was a native of Tu Minh, ever studying the Tiantai contemplations and cultivating Buddha-Recitation Samadhi. In those days Buddhist students often mistook the "mind-only, self-nature" teaching: for Ultimate Bliss, they sought nothing in the West but looked within the discriminating mind. Pitying this sickness born of medicine, the Great Master composed two volumes, "Jewel-King Samadhi: Direct Pointers on Recitation." Through this, erring Chan and Pure Land cultivators found the shore. This was around the 28th year of Hongwu of the Ming. Two hundred years later, Great Master Lianchi admired the work, but it had been lost and he sought it long in vain. Later Chan Master Wanrong chanced upon it and spread it abroad. Great Master Ouyi included it in the "Ten Essentials of the Pure Land.")

*The Great Master taught: — Practitioners vowing to recite the Buddha's name, before entering the practice hall, must reflect: I and all beings ever dwell in the sea of birth-and-death suffering; if I liberate not all, how call it true practice? Hence view foe and kin alike with equality and raise great compassion — then no evil demons or wicked parties can make you retreat. With the great mind established, study the ancients' true recitation practices, set up the practice hall according to Dharma, as solemn and pure as possible. Then, six times day and night, with wholehearted sincerity cast oneself in homage to the Three Jewels, confess every offense, seeking repentance. Kneel before the Buddha, holding incense and flowers in offering, and contemplate throughout the Dharma-realm: I and all beings, from before beginningless time lost in suffering — tears falling in pity — seeking the Buddha's aid, vowing to liberate all kinds. Thus, straining one's strength in bitter practice: if obstacles run deep and no response comes, make death the deadline, allowing not an instant's thought of worldly five-desire joys. Those of lesser faculties, unable to such supreme practice, may still, in a pure hut, keep body and mind solemnly clean and cultivate as they will: timed worship and repentance, vowing vigor without retreat; reciting alone or with mantra and sutra besides. Beholding fine marks, know offenses erased and good ties ripened.

• Question: How apply the mind to be free of scattering? Answer: Use body and mouth in recitation, minding neither essence nor concentration — only keep the Buddha-phrase unbroken, and one-pointedness comes of itself; this may itself be called "one-pointedness." But recite on without cease — as a mother who has lost her child, as a dragon who has lost the life-pearl — then scattering holds no fear; seeking not one-pointedness, one-pointedness comes of itself. Never force the mind to oneness — forced, it never comes; in truth it turns only on the cultivator's diligence or laziness! I grieve that people today mostly cultivate without fruit — shallow faith, untrue practice. Many, never establishing practice, already wish others to know beforehand: inwardly self-satisfied, outwardly boastful, hinting at attainments to win homage. Some even lie of beholding pure realms, or small realms, or fine dream-signs. In truth they cannot tell true realms from false, yet boast wildly. Such base-minded ones demons surely delude; vows and practice slowly retreat, drifting with the stream of birth-and-death. Should this not give pause?

• Cultivators, toward even a small offense, must hold fearful care; understanding may follow the Mahayana, but deeds must copy beginners.

• Cultivators blocked by past karma, their practice waning, should single-mindedly uphold the Rebirth Mantra. This dharani-door uproots every root of karmic obstruction: one recitation erases the body's five rebellious and ten evil offenses; a hundred thousand recitations, and the enlightenment-mind is never forgotten; two hundred thousand, and the enlightenment-sprout stirs to life; three hundred thousand, and Amitabha ever abides upon the crown — rebirth in the Pure Land certain.

---o0o---

noi_dung:
Great Master Konggu

(The Great Master, surnamed Tran, named Canh Long, was a native of Ngo Huyen. As a boy he kept a vegetarian diet and loved sitting upright with eyes closed, like a meditation practitioner. Later he studied the great Dharma under Hoa Thuong Lai Van; at twenty-eight he left home at Ho Khau. Then the Great Master entered Mount Thien Muc, cultivating bitterly in inquiry, until one day he suddenly awakened; seeking confirmation from Lai Van, he was approved. Though awakened to the mind-essence, in self-cultivation and exhorting others he followed the Pure Land throughout. He composed 108 Pure Land verses circulating in the world. He built his own bone-stupa at Tien Duong, writing its inscription himself, and ever cultivated within it until his perfect passing.)

• The Great Master said: — The one door of Buddha-recitation is the straight shortcut of cultivation. Practitioners must see this body as false, worldly affairs as dreams; only the Pure Land is worth refuge, only the recitation worth reliance. Then recite according to your portion — fast or slow, low or loud, all unobstructed. Only keep body and mind free and detached, silently mindful, never forgetting; in leisure or haste, movement or stillness — one thought unchanging. Reciting thus, one day, scenes touching conditions, you will suddenly awaken. Then you will know the Silent-Light Pure Land never leaves this place, Amitabha never outside your mind. To set the mind on seeking awakening becomes itself obstruction — take faith alone as root, follow no stray thoughts. Practiced thus, though unawakened, at death you are still reborn in the West, advancing grade by grade, retrogression no more feared.

• The Great Assembly Sutra says: "Loud recitation carries ten merits: 1) shattering dull sleep; 2) frightening maras; 3) its sound reaching the ten directions; 4) the three evil paths' suffering cut off; 5) outer sounds cannot invade; 6) the reciting mind unscattered; 7) vigorous advance; 8) the Buddhas rejoicing; 9) samadhi manifesting; 10) rebirth in the Pure Land."

---o0o---

noi_dung:
Great Master Zongben

(The Great Master, surnamed Tran, styled Nhat Nguyen, was a native of Tu Minh. As a boy he studied Confucianism, versed in poetry and rites. At fifteen, witnessing the death of his cousin, the recluse Hu Moc, he oft grieved in fear, wishing to leave home and train in the Path to escape birth-and-death samsara. Later, worshiping the Buddha at Tra Dinh in Hang Chau, he met a Chan master, invited him home, made offerings, bowed, and asked the method of cultivation. The Chan master praised him and revealed the Buddha-recitation door. Once ordained, he inquired with all his might and awakened to the true mind, returning to devote himself to the Pure Land. In the Long Khanh years, the Great Master wrote the Direct Pointers on Returning to the Source, spreading the Lotus School. Master Ly Trac Ngo oft sang his virtuous practice. Later the Great Master dwelt in seclusion; the day of his final passing is unknown.)

• The Great Master said: — In reciting the Buddha's name, never mind what kind of person: to think your lifelong evils many and abandon cultivation is error! Never mind what time: to think yourself old, near death, and refuse cultivation is error! Never mind what method: to fix one rigid rule and force all to follow, obstructing their practice, is error. Know that the Pure Land door chooses none — wise or dull, noble or low, rich or poor; no distinction of men or women, old or young, monk or lay; no question of long-trained or newly practicing — all may recite. Loud or soft, voiced or silent, bowing in recitation, inquiring in recitation, gathered-mind in recitation, contemplated in recitation, rosary in recitation, holding the Buddha's name unbroken as flowing water in recitation — walking reciting, standing reciting, sitting reciting, lying reciting, a thousand myriad recitations returning to one recitation. Recite in whatever way — the essentials are holding long and unretreating, with firm and settled faith, seeking rebirth in the West. Practiced truly thus — what need to seek wise teachers to ask the way?

Thus the Pure Land has many methods; the fruit turns on the heart's vow-direction. As they say: "Sailing the boat turns on the helmsman; understanding alike, all return to the lotus land!"

---o0o---

Coming to the capital, Emperor Than Tong held him in high regard, and he memorialized to have the sutra-blocks printed as books. Stern and resolute by nature, wholeheartedly upholding the true Dharma, he drew the jealousy of the wicked...)
noi_dung:
Great Master Zibo

(The Great Master, surnamed Tram, was a native of Cu Khuc. After leaving home he cultivated Chan and Pure Land together, going deep into their subtleties. Coming to the capital, Emperor Than Tong held him in high regard, and he memorialized to have the sutra-blocks printed as books. Stern and resolute by nature, wholeheartedly upholding the true Dharma, he drew the jealousy of the wicked. Before long a memorial of false accusation was submitted; brought to trial, he argued with true reason, his expression natural — yet he was still cast into prison. The magistrate, bribed, sought his harm. The Great Master said: "Since it is so, no need for your hand!" Then, calling for bath-water and speaking a verse, he passed away seated upright. All his life the Great Master taught the Pure Land door most earnestly, saying: "Right mindfulness at life's end depends wholly on deep effort in ordinary days." Seeing the Great Master's freedom in life and death, his ordinary-day cultivation may well be imagined.)

• The Great Master said: — Whether reciters are genuine and earnest in heart may be tested in moments of joy or affliction — here the true and false of the heart show plainly, and may be inferred. In general, those who truly recite, whether amid affliction or joy, keep the recitation unbroken; such scenes cannot move them. Unmoved by these two, at the moment of life and death they are naturally unafraid. Today's reciters, at a breath of gladness or anger, shelve the recitation behind them. How then can recitation prove efficacious? Recite as I say: amid love and hate, never forget one phrase, A Di Đà Phật. Keep it exactly so, and if in the present you do not gain free mastery in practice, and at life's end are not reborn in the West — then may my tongue rot away. Fail as I say, and recitation has no power — the fault is yours, nothing to do with me!

• He further asked the student Hai Chau: "Is your recitation ever broken?" He replied: "Ordinarily I keep it — only closing my eyes in sleep, I forget." The Great Master darkened and rebuked: "Forgetting recitation the moment the eyes close in sleep — ten thousand years will never bring success! From now on, even in sleep and dreams you must keep recitation unbroken to have a share in escaping suffering. Waking to find it forgotten in sleep, weep in grief, bow before the Buddha's altar in repentance, then kneel and recite a thousand or ten thousand calls with all your might. After two or three such rounds, even in slumber the recitation will appear unbroken!"

Editor's note: To recite waking, forgetting only in sleep — as Hai Chau did — is truly rare! The Great Master's rebuke was suited to a high-capacity person, urging one step further toward one-pointedness — not true censure. Beginners must not cling to this and fall into doubt and retreat.

---o0o---

tom_tat: (The Great Master was the Eighth Patriarch of the Lotus School, named Chau Hoang, surnamed Tram, a native of Nhan Hoa. At first he left home under Hoa Thuong Tinh Thien; after receiving the great precepts he traveled widely to study with wise teachers. Worshiping the sacred traces on Mount Wutai, he was moved when Manjushri emitted light. Coming to Yunqi Mountain and finding its scenery secluded, he wished to dwell there all his life...)
noi_dung:
Great Master Lianchi

(The Great Master was the Eighth Patriarch of the Lotus School, named Chau Hoang, surnamed Tram, a native of Nhan Hoa. At first he left home under Hoa Thuong Tinh Thien; after receiving the great precepts he traveled widely to study with wise teachers. Worshiping the sacred traces on Mount Wutai, he was moved when Manjushri emitted light. Coming to Yunqi Mountain and finding its scenery secluded, he wished to dwell there all his life. The mountain folk suffered much from tigers; the Great Master recited sutras and fed the hungry ghosts, and the tigers withdrew. In a drought year, walking the field-paths reciting, rain fell wherever his feet stepped. From then on followers grew daily, and the Great Master gathered them all through recitation. He authored the Yunqi Dharma Collection of twenty-odd works, by and large proclaiming the Pure Land. Before life's end, the Great Master bade farewell to disciples and old friends, urging true recitation. At the appointed time he passed away seated in recitation, at eighty-one.)

• The Great Master said: —Recitation has silent recitation, loud recitation, and vajra recitation. But silent recitation easily sinks into stupor, and loud recitation feels wasting of strength; only the vajra method — lips and tongue faintly moving — can endure long. Yet fix on nothing: when vajra recitation tires, silent recitation is no hindrance; when stupor comes, switch back to loud recitation.

• The mind long scattered cannot settle in a moment; so reciters whose minds are unpure must not fret overmuch — only let each word, each phrase issue from the heart; sustained effort bears fruit of itself.

• Scattered thoughts are the sickness, recitation the medicine; recitation exists precisely to cure scattering — and no effect seen means effort not yet genuine. So when scattered thoughts rise, bend the whole heart to effortful recitation, each word, each phrase concentrated and undistracted — scattering ceases of itself.

• Amid ten thousand tangled thoughts is the very moment to apply effort: the instant scattering comes, swiftly gather it back; continue thus, and in time effort ripens — false thoughts unborn of themselves. Besides, knowing thoughts many comes through recitation; unreciting, the false mind surges like waves, never resting an instant — then how would you know yourself?

• Buddhist students must not over-follow outer forms — only true cultivation is precious. Lay followers at home need not shave heads and wear patched robes — hair uncut, plain dress will do for recitation. Lovers of quiet need not strike bells and wooden fish — silent recitation of themselves will do. Those fearing troublesome ties need not form societies and fellowships — closed doors will do for recitation. The literate need not enter temples to hear sutras — reading sutras themselves and reciting as taught will do. A thousand miles pilgrimaging famous mountains cannot match sitting quietly at home in recitation. Offering to untrue monks cannot match filial care for parents in recitation. Befriending many of weak virtue cannot match an ignorant person's wholehearted recitation. Low conduct mouthing lofty principles cannot match a simple person keeping precepts in recitation. A novelty-loving nature craving demons' psychic powers cannot match true faith in cause and effect in recitation. In short: reciters keeping hearts straight and cutting evil deeds are called good people. Reciters illuminating mind-nature and cutting delusion-karma are called sages.

• I urge the very idle — household and children settled, above and below at leisure — to bend whole hearts to recitation, daily from thousands to ten-thousand calls. I urge those bound by worldly ties — toiling at public duties, hurrying for household affairs — though seldom idle, each dawn to spare a little time, reciting some ten breaths. Besides, whenever idle, intersperse a hundred calls.

• When I was still pilgrimaging for the Path, hearing Chan Master Bianrong's great repute, I went to seek the teaching; two or three times kneeling in inquiry, the Chan Master said: "Keep your own portion, crave not fame and gain, chase not outer ties — only clarify cause and effect and single-mindedly recite, that is all." I received it and withdrew. My fellow pilgrims all laughed: "A thousand miles for this — hoping for lofty, wondrous words, and bringing back phrases not worth half a coin! Who could not say as much!" I replied: "Here lies the Chan Master's goodness. Thirsting in longing from a thousand miles, he spoke no mystifying words to overawe the lowly — only plain, honest, the close-fitting yet essential effort he himself had realized, urging and entrusting. His excellence lies precisely here." To this day I keep those words, daring not forget.

Editor's note: "Keep your portion, crave not fame and gain, follow not outer ties, clarify cause and effect, single-mindedly recite." These words seem shallow and common, yet are truly lofty, deep, wondrous — simple, yet embracing the sutras' meaning, gathering a lifetime's cultivation-essence. Kept exactly — examine closely — how many have done it? The shallow will despise these words; lovers of mystifying principles, deeming themselves supremely unobstructed, will surely never practice them. Had Bianrong never experienced it, he could not have uttered them; had Lianchi not truly cultivated, he could not have received them.

---o0o---

tom_tat: (The Master, named Duc Thanh, surnamed Thai, was a native of Kim Lang. Leaving home at nineteen, he single-mindedly recited the Buddha's name. One night the Great Master dreamed of Amitabha manifesting in the sky. Ever after, he seemed to see the Buddha's image before him...)
noi_dung:
Great Master Hanshan

(The Master, named Duc Thanh, surnamed Thai, was a native of Kim Lang. Leaving home at nineteen, he single-mindedly recited the Buddha's name. One night the Great Master dreamed of Amitabha manifesting in the sky. Ever after, he seemed to see the Buddha's image before him. The Great Master inquired in Chan near ten years; awakened, he withdrew into the Lao Mountains. Before, the folk round about had never heard the true teaching — but soon after his coming, three-year-olds could recite the Buddha's name. The Holy Mother Empress, hearing his fame, took refuge as his disciple with lavish offerings. The jealous slandered him, the king in anger banished the Great Master to Lei Zhou. There he revived the Caoxi practice center. Later the king pardoned and recalled him; the Great Master dwelt at Lei Mountain in pure-karma devotion. Then at Caoxi, reciting, he passed away, at seventy-eight; his flesh-body remains to this day.)

• The Great Master taught: — The most essential point in cultivation is an earnest heart over samsara's revolving birth and death. Without earnestness over birth-and-death, how dare one speak of recitation grown into one seamless whole? If truly earnest over revolving, each thought is as putting out fire on the head — fearing only to lose this human body, ten thousand kalpas hardly regained. Then hold fast the recitation, beat back false thoughts; in every time, every place, the Buddha's name ever present, by no false feelings veiled or dragged. Such bitter effort, long sustained — recitation ripens of itself, mind corresponding; unseeking, reciting power naturally grows into one seamless whole.

• Six times day and night, take one recitation-phrase and settle it upon the heart — each thought unforgotten, each mind undimmed. Then shelve every worldly thought; view the recitation-phrase as your very life — teeth clenched, holding fast, never letting go. Walking, standing, sitting, lying, eating, drinking, working — the phrase ever manifest. Meeting afflictive ties, mind uneasy — only recite wholeheartedly, and affliction melts of itself. For affliction is samsara's root; recitation the ship crossing birth-and-death's sea. To escape birth and death, shatter affliction with the recitation-phrase alone — a simple method, yet most excellent.

• To establish a recitation practice center through the twelve hours, numbers great or small matter not — only divide into shifts, each shift one period, revolving in recitation. Thus six times day and night: as the next shift ascends, this shift, though retired, still recites silently or listens to the companions' Buddha-voices. Kept thus, Buddha-voices unceasing, false thoughts unborn — as travelers in deep darkness, calling to one another, never lost. Then movement and stillness are as one, self and others undifferent. Amitabha ever manifest — no practice-center peace more wondrous than this.

---o0o---

tom_tat: (The Great Master was the Ninth Patriarch of the Lotus School, surnamed Chung, named Tri Huc, a native of Ngo Huyen. His father upheld the Great Compassion Mantra for ten years and dreamed of Avalokiteshvara handing him a child — thus he was born. At first he followed Confucianism, writing books refuting Buddhism; upon reading the Bamboo Window Essays, he burned his own manuscripts...)
noi_dung:
Great Master Ouyi

(The Great Master was the Ninth Patriarch of the Lotus School, surnamed Chung, named Tri Huc, a native of Ngo Huyen. His father upheld the Great Compassion Mantra for ten years and dreamed of Avalokiteshvara handing him a child — thus he was born. At first he followed Confucianism, writing books refuting Buddhism; upon reading the Bamboo Window Essays, he burned his own manuscripts. At twenty-four he left home and trained in Chan; struck by near-fatal sickness, he turned to pure karma. Later, dwelling in seclusion at Linh Phong Monastery, he wrote prolifically. At life's end he bade his body be cremated, the ashes mixed with flour into pellets to feed birds and fish — to form ties with the West — then passed away seated upright. Three years later his disciples opened the shrine: the Great Master's countenance was as in life, his hair grown long covering his ears. Unwilling to follow the will, they built a flesh-stupa enshrined at Linh Phong.)

• The Great Master taught: — The Buddha-recitation door holds nothing strange — only deep faith, earnest vows, and vigorous true practice. The essentials are faith penetrating, holding long, single-minded recitation — daily and nightly a hundred thousand, thirty thousand, or fifty thousand calls, the fixed number never short. Practiced thus a whole life, vowing never to change — if rebirth fails, the Buddhas of the three times speak falsely. Once reborn, retrogression ends, and all Dharma-doors manifest. Most shunned is a mind inconstant — today thus, tomorrow otherwise; hearing some mystifying teaching, chasing after it — then no door succeeds. Know that one phrase, A Di Đà Phật, recited to ripeness, contains the Tripitaka's twelve divisions and the ultimate teachings; contains the seventeen hundred koans and the upward path; contains the three thousand deportments, eighty thousand fine conducts, and the three pure precept-groups.

• True reciters, casting off body, mind, and world, practice great giving; no more greed, anger, and delusion arising is great precept-keeping; no more reckoning right and wrong, winning and losing is great forbearance; unbroken and unmixed is great vigor; no wandering thoughts loosed is great meditation; unbeguiled by other paths is great wisdom. Examine yourselves: if body, mind, and world are still unabandoned, thoughts of greed, anger, and delusion still arising, rights and wrongs still weighed at heart, wandering thoughts still unquelled, other paths still beguiling the will — such are not called true reciters.

• For the state of "one mind unconfused," there is no strange device. Beginning effort requires rosary and count: daily and nightly a fixed number, never short. Kept exactly thus, long sustained, reciting power ripens into "reciting without reciting" — then counting or not is free. To crave lofty words at the outset — marklessness, perfect interfusion and freedom — reciting power can hardly form. That is shallow faith, effort not full: though you could expound the twelve divisions and penetrate seventeen hundred koans, all belongs to samsara's shore — at life's end, of no use.

• Recitation has phenomenal holding and noumenal holding. Phenomenal holding: believing Amitabha stands in the West, not yet understanding this very mind makes Buddha — only resolved to be reborn, reciting as a child remembers its mother, never for a moment forgetting. Noumenal holding: believing Amitabha of the West is one's own mind fully endowed, created by one's own mind — taking this self-endowed, self-created red name as the object binding the heart, never for a moment forgetting.

---o0o---

tom_tat: (The Great Master was the Tenth Patriarch of the Lotus School, surnamed Tuong, named Hanh Sach, a native of Nghi Nhon. He left home at twenty-three, devoted to pure karma, ever presiding at Tay Khe Monastery in Hang Chau to spread the Pure school, his teaching most flourishing. He composed the Lotus Treasury Collection and Pure Land Dharma Words, circulating in the world...)
noi_dung:
Great Master Cheliu

(The Great Master was the Tenth Patriarch of the Lotus School, surnamed Tuong, named Hanh Sach, a native of Nghi Nhon. He left home at twenty-three, devoted to pure karma, ever presiding at Tay Khe Monastery in Hang Chau to spread the Pure school, his teaching most flourishing. He composed the Lotus Treasury Collection and Pure Land Dharma Words, circulating in the world. In the 21st year of Kangxi he manifested passing, at fifty-five. At that time a clansman of the imperial house and a son of the Ngo family died together; after a day both revived, telling alike: "The underworld officers seized and bound me beneath the court — suddenly radiance blazed everywhere, fragrance, blossoms, and jewels filling the sky. The Dark King prostrated, escorting a Great Master to the West — looking closely, it was Master Che. By that radiance I was pardoned and returned.")

• The Great Master said: — Name-holding practice prizes one mind unconfused, unmixed — not speed or multitude. Only hold recitation thought upon thought in succession, neither hurried nor slow, letting the Buddha's name stand distinct and clear in the heart. Eating, dressing, walking, standing, sitting, lying — one red-name phrase linked unbroken as the breath, unscattered, unsunk. Holding thus may be called one-pointed vigor on one's own portion.

• Today's pure-karma cultivators recite all day, repent, vow — yet the West stays distant, rebirth unassured. Why? Outwardly bowing, reciting, vowing — inwardly love-threads still tightly bound, affection-roots still deep! See Saha's worldly love as impermanent, false, like chewing wax: whether in leisure or haste, movement or stillness, joy or pain, care or gladness — hold one Buddha-name phrase fast as leaning on Mount Sumeru; no circumstance can move it. Feeling weary, lax, afflictions arising — rouse one heart and recite, like a long sword propping heaven, scattering the demon-armies of affliction traceless, like red fire in the forge melting consciousness and feeling since beginninglessness. Whoever keeps thus — though presently in the five turbidities, the whole body already sits in the lotus world. What need wait for Amitabha's extended hand, Avalokiteshvara's leading, to believe oneself reborn?

Editor's note: The Records of Pure Land Sages lists Master Xing'an as Tenth Patriarch, but later Great Master Yinguang and Pure Land cultivators, seeing Master Cheliu's lofty succession and flourishing teaching, his great merit to the Lotus School, honored him as Tenth Patriarch, making Master Xing'an the Eleventh. Noted here to resolve doubt — Lien Du.

---o0o---

tom_tat: (The Master, styled Vi Lam, surnamed Dinh, was a native of An Nhon. He left home at fourteen and lectured widely. Later coming to Co Son, he followed Chan Master Vinh Giac in inquiry for three years without awakening. Bidding farewell, he wandered through Luong Triet and returned to Co Son to cultivate. One day, lifting a curtain, he greatly awakened...)
noi_dung:
Great Master Daopai

(The Master, styled Vi Lam, surnamed Dinh, was a native of An Nhon. He left home at fourteen and lectured widely. Later coming to Co Son, he followed Chan Master Vinh Giac in inquiry for three years without awakening. Bidding farewell, he wandered through Luong Triet and returned to Co Son to cultivate. One day, lifting a curtain, he greatly awakened. In the 14th year of Shunzhi of the Qing, the Great Master succeeded Vinh Giac, opening the Dharma to beings for more than twenty years. The Chan forest honored him as foremost in Buddha-Dharma in the Southeast. He composed the Pure Land Decisive Pointers. He oft said: "This old monk's aspiration lies in Chan, his practice in the Pure Land." Later dwelling in seclusion, his final passing is unknown.)

• The Great Master taught: — In reciting, the heart must never part from two words, "faith and remembrance"; the mouth never part from two words, "calling and reverence." For reaching the Pure Land requires a faithful heart: a thousand believing, a thousand reborn; ten thousand believing, ten thousand returning. If the heart ever faithfully remembers the Buddha and the mouth ever earnestly, reverently calls the Buddha, the Buddha will surely save. This is called deep faith!

• In reciting, each word must be distinct, each phrase linked to the next — indistinctness is stupor, unlinkage is scattering. Practiced thus, one recitation-phrase ever distinct in the heart; in time, Buddha-Recitation Samadhi ripens of itself.

---o0o---

tom_tat: (The Great Master was the Tenth Patriarch of the Lotus School, surnamed Thoi, styled Tu Te, a native of Thuong Thuc. He left home at seven, received the great precepts at twenty-four, and penetrated Chan, doctrine, nature, and marks alike. Dwelling at Chan Tich Monastery, he read the canon and recited the Buddha's name. After three years, his eloquence flowed like a cataract...)
noi_dung:
Great Master Xing'an

(The Great Master was the Tenth Patriarch of the Lotus School, surnamed Thoi, styled Tu Te, a native of Thuong Thuc. He left home at seven, received the great precepts at twenty-four, and penetrated Chan, doctrine, nature, and marks alike. Dwelling at Chan Tich Monastery, he read the canon and recited the Buddha's name. After three years, his eloquence flowed like a cataract. He further visited Duc Vuong Monastery to worship the stupas, and was moved when relics emitted light; thereupon he composed the Nirvana Repentance and the Exhortation to the Bodhi-Mind, at which readers often shed tears. In old age, the Great Master dwelt at Pham Thien Monastery in Hang Chau, founding a lotus society for mutual encouragement in pure-karma devotion. In winter of the 11th year of Yongzheng, the Great Master foresaw that on the 14th day of the fourth month next year he would be reborn. At the appointed time he said: "Ten days ago I already beheld the Buddha; now I behold him again." Speaking thus, he recited and returned to the West.)

• The Great Master said: "One word, vow, embraces both faith and practice. Faith means trusting: self, other, cause, effect, phenomenon, principle — none falsely. Faith in self: trusting all is mind-made, that my recitation will win reception. Faith in other: trusting Shakyamuni speaks no falsehood, Amitabha vows in no emptiness. Faith in cause: trusting recitation is the cause of rebirth and liberation. Faith in effect: trusting rebirth and Buddhahood are the fruit. Faith in phenomenon: trusting the Western realm, every mark, is wholly real. Faith in principle: trusting the mind-only true nature enfolds the Buddha-land. Each point above is certain — hence called unfalse. Practice means holding the Name alone, unmixed, unscattered. Vow means each heart delighting, each thought aspiring. Of these three conditions, pure-karma cultivators must have all — none may lack — and 'vow' is the vital point. There may be faith and practice without vow; there has never been vow without faith and practice.

• Reciting without giving rise to the enlightenment-mind does not correspond with Amitabha's primal vow, and rebirth is hard to win. (The enlightenment-mind is the heart benefiting self and others — above seeking Buddhahood, below vowing to liberate beings.) Yet giving rise to the enlightenment-mind without single-minded recitation likewise wins no rebirth. Take the enlightenment-mind as principal cause, recitation as supporting condition, then seek rebirth in the Pure Land. Pure-karma cultivators must understand this.

• Recitation too has demonic workings — from three causes: unclear doctrine, no good teachers and friends, no self-examination. Of the three, examining one's own errors is most vital. In general, rebirth in the West is not won with a little blessing, a little lax practice; escaping ten thousand kalpas of revolving birth-and-death suffering is not won with a procrastinating, ever-deferring, lazy heart! Impermanence is swift — morning follows night in a breath; should we not diligently prepare beforehand! I only fear vows weaker than sentimental love, reciting thoughts weaker than dusty desires — and for those ever lax and half-believing, I too know not what to do!

A verse says:

Nam Mô A Di Đà,

Who does not know to recite?

Yet reciting, uncorresponding,

Mother and child hard to meet!

Walking, standing, sitting, lying,

Gather this mind in;

Each thought succeeding thought,

Long reciting grows into one whole.

Thus reciting Amitabha,

Amitabha manifests of himself!

Rebirth in the West decided,

All life, never retreating!

noi_dung:
Great Master Chewu

(The Great Master was the Twelfth Patriarch of the Lotus School, surnamed Ma, named Te Tinh, a native of Phong Nhuan. Leaving home at twenty-two, he penetrated Chan and doctrine alike. At first he presided at Van Tho Monastery in Beijing, his fame spreading north and south, ever proclaiming the Pure Land door and urging pure cultivation. Next the Great Master presided at Giac Sanh Monastery, his renown as resounding as before. Later, dwelling on Mount Hong Loa, ever more multitudes turned to him — a Pure Land practice center formed. Under the Qing, in spring of the 15th year of Jiaqing, the Great Master foretold his western return, saying: "This illusory body does not last — let no life pass in vain; all should strive in recitation." At the appointed day, the Great Master saw the Buddha come to receive him, and passed away seated in right mindfulness. The assembly smelled a strange rich fragrance; at the cremation more than a hundred relics were found.)

• The Great Master said: — "Truly for birth and death, give rise to the enlightenment-mind; with deep faith and vows, hold the Buddha's name" — these sixteen words are the guiding essence of the recitation door. Without a genuine earnest heart over birth-and-death, all guidance is empty words. For of this life's sufferings none exceeds birth and death: since beginningless kalpas we have lived and died, died and lived — leaving this womb to enter the next, casting this skin to wear another — suffering unbearable. How much more, ourselves unescaped from revolving, how avoid falling? Alas! One erring thought, and down into evil paths — the three realms easy to enter, hard to leave; hell's days long, its pains heavy! So let the assembly ache over birth and death — as mourning parents, as putting out fire on the head — striving in keen cultivation. Yet grieving birth-and-death and seeking escape, think of all the myriad kinds alike. Beings and I share one essence — my parents through many kalpas, Buddhas of future ages. Without a liberating heart, seeking escape alone — toward feeling, uneasy; toward principle, lacking. How much more: without the great heart, outwardly no stimulus-response with the Buddha, inwardly no joining with the true nature; above, Buddhahood unrounded; below, the myriad kinds unliberated. How then repay many kalpas of kindness, how resolve many lives of enmity, how mature roots planted of old, how repent offenses made before? Then practice meets obstructing ties everywhere, and even success bears low fruit. Therefore accord with nature and give rise to the enlightenment-mind.

With the great heart given rise to, true practice must be cultivated — and among all practice-doors, seeking the method easiest to apply, swiftest to mature, most secure, most perfect-and-sudden, nothing exceeds deep faith and vows holding the Buddha's name. Holding the Name means keeping the Buddha's name firm in the heart, never for a moment forgetting. One broken thought, one mixed thought — not called holding. Keeping thought upon thought unbroken, unmixed — this is true vigor; vigor unceasing ripens in time into one mind unconfused, perfecting pure karma. One mind unconfused is pure karma's final refuge, the Pure Land's great gate — unentered, never secure. Should students not strive?

• The mind that can make karma can also turn karma; karma made by mind must follow mind in turning. If my mind cannot turn karma, karma binds it; if karma does not follow mind, it can bind mind. But how to use the mind to turn karma? By keeping the mind joined to morality, joined to the Buddha. And how does karma bind the mind? By letting the mind follow old roads, loosed among dusty realms.

• All realms now, all retribution hereafter, are karma-summoned, mind-manifest. Karma-summoned, coming retribution is fixed — karma binding mind. Mind-manifest, coming retribution is unfixed — mind turning karma. As one whom karma binds to mind, retribution coming fixed — yet suddenly broadening the heart, cultivating true practice — mind turns karma, and the fixed-to-come grows unfixed. If midway the great heart retreats, true practice waning — karma binds mind again, the unfixed-to-come fixing.

But karma made before is done and past — hope lies only in a broadening heart to transform it, and holding that mechanism is I, no other. If today I vow recitation for rebirth in Ultimate Bliss, swiftly to realize the fruit and liberate beings, keeping the Buddha's name unbroken thought upon thought — in time the heart joins the Path, turning Saha's retribution-fruit into Ultimate Bliss, exchanging a fleshly womb for a lotus womb; before long I myself shall be a superior good person, fine-marked, solemn, blissful, and free in the seven-jeweled lotus land. If midway I slowly lax and retreat, past-life karma's mighty power dispatches me, and I remain as before — enduring measureless bodily and mental pains, a hungry ghost, an animal. Whoever aspires to escape, seeking the Pure Land — should they not fear, awaken, rouse the heart, and cultivate?

• Eight essentials pure-karma cultivators should remember:

For birth and death, give rise to the enlightenment-mind — the common road of Path-students.

With deep faith and vows, hold the Buddha's name — the true essence of the Pure Land door.

Gathered-mind, concentrated recitation as expedient effort.

Subduing present afflictions as the mind-work essential.

Holding the four weighty precepts as the Path-entry root.

Bitter austerities as cultivation aids.

One mind unconfused as the Pure Land door's final refuge.

Auspicious signs as rebirth's proof.

noi_dung:
Great Master Wukai

(The Great Master, surnamed Truong, styled Hoat Nhien, was a native of To Chau. He left home and cultivated at Tuong Phong Monastery. Awakening to the three essentials, he opened the teaching at Hien Than Monastery in Kinh Nam. Retiring into seclusion, he passed through the temples of Van Gian and Luyen Xuyen, then returned to the Bao Tang hermitage to devote himself to pure karma. He authored the Hundred Questions on Recitation, Knowledge for Beginning Pure-Karma Practice, the Recitation Mirror-Warnings, First Lessons for Pure-Karma Beginners, and Old Way Feelings. In the 10th year of Daoguang of the Qing, feeling sick, he urged the assembly and foretold that past autumn's end he would return to the West. Indeed, two days before the Start of Winter, the Great Master faced west, recited, and passed away.)

The Great Master said: — Reciting with eyes open, the mind easily scatters — so close the eyes in recitation. Before reciting, sit quiet a moment, cast off everything, empty the heart, then slowly proclaim the Buddha's name — reciting while listening, listening while reciting, silently reciting in succession; practiced long, the heart issues forth, each phrase earnestly longing for the Pure Land. There is a tying-mindfulness method: when not reciting, bind your mindful heart upon Amitabha Buddha's body. Thus the mind grows pure, unmoved — the very place of effective effort.

Question: Whence arise scattered thoughts? Answer: My heart holds but one thought — reciting is it, and scattered thoughts are it too. Only my recitation is not yet concentrated, so dusty thoughts still drift — that is all.

Question: How to dispel scattered thoughts?

Answer: No need to dispel them — only place the whole mindful heart upon the Buddha's name, and scattered thoughts vanish.

Question: But with weak, failing energy, unable to make them vanish — then what?

Answer: Virtue unripe means much scattering — gather the six senses gradually toward purity. If not yet possible, open the eyes and gaze steadily at the Buddha's image in recitation — scattered thoughts dissolve.

Question: That method is good — but fearing fatigue returns and scattered thoughts rise again — then what?

Answer: The heart dim means outer circumstances drag it; recitation powerless, even false thoughts dense and undispersed. But never hurry in haste — settle the mind, recite slowly: the Buddha's name issuing from the heart, sounding at the mouth, entering at the ear; heart thinking, mouth reciting, ear hearing — revolving thus, scattered thoughts cease.

Question: This method is excellent — but fearing those of dullest faculties cannot do it — then what?

Answer: Take the six words Nam Mô A Di Đà Phật in recitation. Reciting, note distinctly the first sound, Nam, the second, Mô — thus through all six words, linked unbroken — and false thoughts have nowhere to arise.

noi_dung:
Great Master Miaokong

(The Great Master, surnamed Trinh, was a native of Giang Do. In youth he studied Confucianism, often joining Dharma Master Quan Nhu, Duong Nhu Son, Hua Van Hu and others in planning to carve the Great Canon. Then he left home, styling himself the Sutra-Carving Monk. In fifteen years the Great Master carved more than three thousand volumes; three years after his passing, the Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra was completed. The Great Master kept the precepts strictly — past noon, no eating. All his life he wrote prolifically, later gathered as the Loft of Writings Collection — mostly proclaiming the Pure Land school. He transformed a great multitude, many of them eminent figures such as Tuong Nguyen Luong. In the 6th year of Guangxu of the Qing, the Great Master passed away reciting the Buddha's name, at fifty-five.)

The Great Master said: — Contemplation is not easily accomplished, precepts not easily kept in full, blessings not ripened in a morning or evening, wondrous awakening not for the dull-rooted. And firm great vows are rarer still! Without true Name-holding to find the way out, one must sink in the sea of suffering, ever enduring samsara — a thousand Buddhas in compassion could hardly save! How much more: Name-holding gathers in all three capacities — no expedient surpasses it!

Reciters must neither chatter idly nor let thoughts drift. Slipping into it, reflect: I am a reciter — this is unseemly — then recite a few calls to warn yourself and scatter it.

The "accordant Name-holding" method: drowsy, walk in meditation; scattered, sit again — standing or lying, all free — reciting so the Buddha-phrase never parts. This is the essential art for subduing mind-demons.

Meeting favorable or adverse circumstances, bitter or joyful, right or wrong, gain or loss, foul or pure — every case — hold one recitation-phrase fast. Otherwise circumstances tie you, the Buddha's name breaks off — how pitiable!

• Before the Buddha's image, view that image as the true Buddha — eyes gazing, heart mindful, reverent and utterly sincere. Absent from the image, be reverent still as before the image. Reciting thus, stimulus-response comes easily, evil karma swiftly erased.

All sufferers in life, body and mind unfree, find cultivation hard. Now with some leisure, having heard the recitation door — strive to gather the mind, lest an inch of shadow worth a thousand gold be wasted! Lax cultivation bears hardly any fruit — betraying the four kindnesses, idling the days away; when impermanence suddenly comes, what will withstand it?

Cultivators meeting bitter fruit — past or present lives have planted evil causes. So bearing one part of suffering repays one part of my own evil. Never blame heaven or people for unfairness, nor fortune for turning upside down — only shame myself for late awakening to cultivation. Each such thought — both fearing evil retribution and pitying my own portion — each recitation-phrase issuing from liver and marrow — this is recitation's true state.

Before adversity and suffering, unmoved is inhuman; yet vainly moved — is that one who penetrates Buddha-nature? So, moved, seek the way out of suffering, devise rescue for self and all beings — then not in vain. Know the Buddha is called greatly compassionate because he holds heroic power and wisdom, rescuing beings' pains. With compassionate heart I recite, seeking the Buddha's compassionate rescue from suffering for me — how earnest such holding!

When recitation ripens, among the six dusts only sound-dust remains; the six senses' functions all lodge in the ear-sense — no more knowing the body circumambulating, the tongue moving, thought discriminating or not, the nose breathing out or in, the eyes closed or open. Then Avalokiteshvara's and Mahasthamaprapta's perfect penetration are one: sense is dust, dust is sense, sense-dust is consciousness — the eighteen realms merging into one realm. Finishing a task, speaking a sentence — before reciting-thought rises, one red-name phrase gushes forth unceasing — the sign samadhi easily ripens.

Pure-karma cultivation: solitude — the more, the better; reciting-voice high or low, fast or slow, as suits — joining into one whole. Know then: the body solitary, the heart not lonely — for the Buddhas' hearts and Amitabha's never part from you an instant; your thought rises, the Buddha knows; your mouth opens, the Buddha hears. What fear of solitude?

Sickness is the step toward death; death the pass leading to pure or impure realms, sage or mortal. In sickness, imagine death near, single-mindedly recite, resolved to await life's end — then radiance receives you, fulfilling your rebirth vow. Pausing recitation then — clinging love, grief, fear, all scattered thoughts appear — how cross birth-and-death's road? So in grave sickness remember four words, A Di Đà Phật, in the heart unforgotten — and those around should recite those four words, ever reminding the sick. Know: a hundred kalpas, a thousand lives — rising or falling turns wholly on one thought at that moment. Why? The six paths of revolving all take one thought as master. One thought concentrated on the Buddha — form ruined, spirit unruined — relying on it, rebirth follows. O pure-karma cultivators! Remember four words, A Di Đà Phật, in the heart unforgotten!

noi_dung:
Great Master Yinguang

(The Great Master was the Thirteenth Patriarch of the Lotus School, surnamed Trieu, a native of Cap Duong. He penetrated the teachings and devoted himself to pure karma, dwelling on Mounts Chung Nam, Hong Loa, and Pho Da. In the 19th year of the Republic he came to Ngo, founding the Linh Nham Pure School practice center, urging people to take Confucian duties and cause-and-effect as foundation and Buddha-recitation for rebirth in the West as refuge. The Great Master printed and gave away five million Buddhist books and over a million Buddha images. In winter of the 29th year of the Republic, reciting the Buddha's name, he passed away seated at the Linh Nham center. At the cremation his thirty-two teeth remained whole, with several thousand five-colored relics. The Great Master lived eighty years, sixty as a monk, wrote hundreds of thousands of words, and had more than two hundred thousand disciples — many of them sages and notables of the Nationalist Party.)

The Great Master said: —The Pure Land door was established by Shakyamuni and Amitabha Buddhas, pointed home by the Bodhisattvas Manjushri and Samantabhadra, spread by Ashvaghosha and Nagarjuna, and proclaimed by the Patriarchs Huiyuan, Tiantai, Qingliang, Yongming, Lianchi, and Ouyi — urging saints and mortals, dull and wise alike to cultivate together.

Pure-karma cultivators must uphold human duties, fulfill every station, end deviant thoughts, guard a sincere and reverent heart, abandon all evils, practice all goods, kill nothing, strive to eat vegetarian, cherish and protect living creatures, and with faith and vows recite the Buddha's name seeking rebirth in the West. Within — for grandparents, parents, siblings; without — for kin, friends, neighbors, villages — offer them this Pure Land door in encouragement. Never mind whether they believe and practice or not — only exhaust your own strength to let all know this wondrous Dharma.

Reciters of genuine earnest heart may rely on the Buddha's compassionate power to escape calamities of sword, flood, and fire. Even with deep past karma — or where hell's heavy fruit is turned into this life's light retribution and such calamity chances to strike — if in ordinary days faith and vows were genuine, at that moment the Buddha's reception is certain.

With deep faith and earnest vows, cultivate the principal practice of recitation. Practice here follows each one's station — fix on no single form. Those untied by duties may from dawn to dusk, dusk to dawn — walking, standing, sitting, lying, speaking, silent, moving, still, eating, dressing, relieving nature — in every time, every place keep one red-name phrase never parted from heart and mouth. Body clean, dress neat, place pure — silent or voiced recitation alike. In sleep, undressed, bathing, relieving nature, or in unclean places — silent recitation only, never voiced; silent merit is equal, voiced is irreverent fault. Never think such times unsuited to recitation — fear only failing to recite. Lying down voicing harms not only reverence but the breath — know this.

For a heart unattached to outer things and recitation gathered to oneness, there is no strange method — only never forget death lurking beside you, none knowing its hour.

Reflect: since before beginning I have made measureless, boundless evil karma — as the sutra says, "Were that evil karma formed, the ten directions' void could not contain it." By what luck have I now a human body and heard the Buddha's teaching? Without one heart reciting for rebirth in the West, when death strikes suddenly, falling into evil paths is certain. Then hell's sword-mountains, knife-forests, fire-furnaces, oil-cauldrons — ten thousand living-and-dying in a day and night, pains ultimate beyond telling. Hungry ghosts — forms ugly and foul, bellies drum-large, throats needle-small; seeing food and drink, all turns to fiery coals — hunger and thirst, rolling and wailing through measureless kalpas. Animals — hauling heavy loads, slaughtered for meat, the strong devouring the weak in terror never at rest. Suffering thus — measureless Buddhas appearing in the world, still revolving in evil paths, no escape. Think on the body's fragility, death's uncertainty; think on this life's measureless evil karma made before; think on the three evil paths' pains — awakening in fear — then no more clinging to illusory scenes, recitation single.

In reciting, sincerity is required; sometimes the heart wells with tender grief — a sign roots ripening manifest. But guard against it becoming habitual — else the demon of grief enters. Meeting pleasing things, never overjoy — overjoy invites the demon of elation to enter and obscure.

In reciting, lower the eyelids; never over-strain the spirit — over-straining sends fire-energy upward: headache, dizziness, or hypertension, head numbing, itching, aching, blood congesting at the crown. Regulate to measure. Head heavy and hot — settle the spirit, listen closely in recitation, or contemplate the soles — fire-energy descends.

Sickness and demonic breaking both come from past karma. Sincerely, earnestly recite — sickness self-heals, demons self-withdraw. Insincere, with lustful deviant thoughts arising — your heart wholly sunk in darkness — how escape demons' harassment? From now after each session, dedicate, praying for past-life creditors — through your recitation-merit may they escape suffering, reborn in good realms.

Reciters vigorous and keen — recitation ripens to oneness, resonance with the Buddha, auspicious scenes beheld of themselves — unseen, no hindrance. Abandoning concentrated effort, hasting for one-pointedness, for response, for fine visions — false thoughts tangled, craving knotted at heart — this is cultivators' grave perilous sickness. Long thus, past-life creditors ride your false thoughts, transforming into Buddha-bodies, lotuses, or strange fine scenes, seeking revenge. Then self without right view, wholly of demonic temper — seeing such scenes, joy arising, demons enter the heart's dwelling through it, driving the practitioner mad — a living Buddha could not save.

Reciters must not cultivate outer marks alone — heed dispelling afflictions and habitual errors. Afflictions lessened one part, reciting effort grows one part; afflictions growing, practice must wane. So some cultivate more and "topple karma" more — for this reason; long sustained, karma melts away. From now, in heart-thought and conduct, keep gentleness and kindness — blessings come. Else adding deceit, craft, harshness, treachery — like a bare rocky peak: however it rains, nothing pools; whatever plants, none grow.

Keep one phrase A Di Đà Phật, reciting thought upon thought, ever remembering, ever reciting. When greedy, miserly, wrathful, lustful, contentious, arrogant hearts suddenly rise — think: "I am a reciter seeking liberation — such thoughts unseemly" — thinking, dispel them. Thus, in time, mind-wearying, body-wasting thoughts have nowhere to rise — the Buddha's inconceivable merit-blessing upon your body and mind. I guarantee great effect in ten days. Lax, broken practice craving effect — deceiving self and others; though merit exists, curing sickness thereby is surely impossible.

Whatever done, take sincerity as root — cultivation without a sincere heart, how gain healing benefit, suffering ended?

Pure-karma cultivators: whatever small good merit, all dedicate to rebirth. Then every practice-door aids the Pure Land. Further give rise to the enlightenment-mind, vowing to liberate all kinds, dedicating your cultivated merit to the four kindnesses, three realms, and Dharma-realm beings. Thus — lamp added with oil, seedlings rained upon — forming deep Dharma-ties with all beings, swiftly maturing your own Mahayana supreme practice. Missing this meaning, one falls into the narrow self-benefit views of ordinary folk and the Two Vehicles — cultivating wondrous practice, reaping low fruit.

One secret, earnestly passed on: "Utter sincerity and reverence" — wondrous, wondrous!

Note: Whatever good done, however small, join palms before the Buddha — or facing west — and read this brief dedication verse.

I vow this merit to serve

The four kindnesses, three realms;

I with all beings together

Reborn in Ultimate Bliss.

Great Master Hongyi

(The Great Master, surnamed Ly, named Dien Am, styled Thuc Dong, once studied fine arts in Japan and taught at many schools in China. In the 7th year of the Republic he left home at Dai Tu Monastery in Hang Chau, later receiving the great precepts at Linh An Monastery. Feeling vinaya-study declined, he vowed its revival. Hence wandering through Man and Triet, devoted to lecturing, he authored the Nanshan Vinaya Garden Collection circulating in the world. He devoted himself to pure karma, greatly admiring Yinguang of Linh Nham, ever taking "living to spread the vinaya, dying to be reborn in the West" as his vow. In autumn of the 31st year of the Republic, at On Lang, foreseeing life's end, reciting, he passed away — sixty-four years of age, twenty-four as a monk. After cremation, more than 1,800 relics were found.)

• The Great Master taught: — An old verse says: "I see others die; my heart burns with pity — not pitying the lost, for my turn will come." Life's last great matter — dare it slip the mind an instant!

• Gravely sick, cast off all household matters down to body and mind — single-mindedly recite, one heart aspiring to rebirth in the West. Thus, lifespan ended — rebirth certain. Lifespan unended — though seeking rebirth, sickness swiftly heals instead — for a concentrated heart can erase past evil karma. But uncasting ten thousand ties, unsingle-minded — lifespan ended, rebirth surely missed — for you sought healing, not rebirth; whence the West? Lifespan unended — not only unhealed swiftly, sickness worsens — for craving healing breeds worried fear.

• Sickness not yet grave — medicines allowed, but still keen recitation — never think medicines will heal. Sickness grave — medicines may be refused. Lying sick in my stone hut, one urged inviting a doctor — I declined with this verse:

"A Di Đà Phật, supreme king of healers — not seeking here is folly! One recitation-phrase, the agaḍa medicine — not drinking here is grave error!".

For in ordinary days I trusted the recitation door, explaining it fully to all. Now sick myself, abandoning it for medicine — how?

• Sickness worsening, pains extreme — never panic — for this suffering comes from past karma, or through cultivation turning the evil paths' retribution into light sick-suffering — repaid in full, then reborn in the West.

• Gravely sick, give your clothes and goods to others — or, following the Ksitigarbha Sutra's "Praise of the Tathagata" chapter, offering such goods to sutras and images is better still.

• When the sick suffers much, spirit still clear — family should invite a wise teacher to teach. The wise teacher must comfort fully, recounting the sick person's goods and cultivation with praise — gladdening the sick heart past doubt, self-knowing at death to rely on that good karma reborn in the West.

• When the sick nears death, kin must ask nothing of wills, speak no idle chatter — moving the sick heart to sentimental love, clinging to the world — obstructing rebirth. For wills, in healthy days write testamentary words beforehand, entrusted to keeping.

• Near the end, the sick wishing washing and change — comply, but gently, carefully. Unwilling, or speechless — never force. For the dying oft ache through the body — forced moving, washing, changing increases pain. In this world, cultivators vowing the West, at life's end by kin moved and disturbed, right mindfulness broken, miss rebirth — such cases many. Some dying might reach good realms, but the ignorant touching, pain arising — anger arising — falling into evil paths. Like King Ajatashatru, much-blessed, at life's end when a drowsy attendant dropped a fan upon his face — angered, died, fell as a python. A mirror — should we not fear and take warning!

• At life's end, sitting or lying — all free, never straining. Feeling breath failing, lying only — yet straining to sit for show is perilous, unwise. By rule lying on the right side facing west — but body aching, supine or on the left side facing east — leave natural, never strain. The sick themselves must understand and manage accordingly. Kin too must understand — never fame-seeking, forcing right-sided western lying, or propping the patient up to don robes, seated in full lotus. Know: craving a little empty fame dooms the dead to the three evil paths, enduring measureless suffering.

• When the assembly aids recitation, invite a receiving-Amitabha image before the sick — letting them behold it.

• Aiders, many or few — if many, take turns in recitation — Buddha-voices unbroken. Four words or six, fast or slow — ask the sick beforehand. Follow the sick person's ordinary accustomed preference in recitation — letting them silently follow. Oft aiders, not for the dying, recite as they please. Against the sick person's accustomed liking — how silently follow? May aiders note this well! Breaking another's right mindfulness is offense — at your own life's end, retribution meets another's breaking, missing rebirth!

• Commonly aiders strike the qing (stone chime) or the small wooden fish. By experience, the sick, nerves weak, greatly fear the qing and small wooden fish — their shrill ear-piercing tones overstimulate the nerves, unsettling hearts. In my humble view, plain recitation suits best. Or if any — only great bells, qing, or large wooden fish — their deep, resonant sounds rousing reverent thoughts in the sick, far better than small chimes and small wooden fish. A dull-toned wooden fish likewise avoid — clouding the sick heart. Tastes differ — better ask the sick beforehand. Mismatched anywhere, adapt with skill, never stubborn.

• Newly breath-ended, the essentials: never hastily move — soiled body, never hastily wash — wait eight hours before bathing and changing. Before and after death, family must not wail — wailing is vain and harmful — stirring clinging in the departed, liberation blocked. Only strive in recitation — true benefit to the dead. To wail, wait eight hours. Why? Breath ended, the alaya-consciousness not yet gone. Then moving, washing, changing, or wailing — pain still felt, or grief-anger, pity-clinging arising — falling far. This matters greatly, needs heed — remember well.

• The theory of probing warmth to judge destinations has evidence — yet never cling. The sick of ordinary true faith and vows, at life's end right mindfulness clear — proof enough of rebirth. Many unskilled, ever probing — shifting here and there, moving the departed's thoughts — great harm too. Breath ended, aiding done — shut the room, guard carefully — lest cats or the unknowing rush in touching — after eight hours bathe and change. Within eight hours, one nearby ever reciting is excellent — all else strictly forbidden. Repeat: in this interval, the dead still feel!

• After eight hours, limbs stiff unmoving — wrap joints in hot-water wrung cloth — soon limbs bend as usual.

• In memorial Buddha-rites for the dead, dedicate that merit to Dharma-realm beings. Thus merit greater, the departed's benefit increased.

• Life's end is life's most critical moment — provisions for rebirth unprepared beforehand, then panic and confusion unavoidable — crying mother, calling father, many kalpas' evil karma manifesting together — how liberation? So at life's end, though aided by others' method, oneself in ordinary days must strive in practice — then self-mastery. O pure-karma cultivators! Prepare early — better!

Homeland of Ultimate Bliss. Vietnamese translation: Venerable Thich Thien Tam.

Typed by: Tue Cuong

THE END
